articles.title: I Fixed WebGPU on Linux. Then Forgot How I Did It.
articles.description: I spent a ridiculous amount of time trying to get WebGPU working properly on my Linux machine.  I...
articles.body_html:
I spent a ridiculous amount of time trying to get WebGPU working properly on my Linux machine.

I eventually figured it out, wrote a script to launch Chrome with all the necessary flags, and even made a desktop launcher so I could just click an icon whenever I wanted to run browser-based AI models.

Problem solved.

Except recently, I started thinking about all the trouble I'd gone through and realized something.

I couldn't remember how I'd fixed it.

Actually, I couldn't even remember where I'd saved the script.

So I did what any reasonable developer would do in 2026. I sent an AI agent to search my computer for code I'd written myself.

And what did it find?

Not only had I saved the script, I'd also written documentation explaining how it worked and backed everything up in TWO different resource directories.

Apparently, past me was considerably more organized than present me remembered.

Anyway, since I've already done all the hard work (and then forgotten about it), I figured I might as well share what I learned.

I just wanted to run AI models in my browser

I've spent quite a bit of time experimenting with local AI models, particularly small language models running through Transformers.js and ONNX Runtime.

I love the idea of running models directly in the browser. No server to maintain, no API calls to pay for, and inference happens right on your own hardware.

WebGPU makes a lot of that possible by allowing web applications to use the GPU for computation.

Which sounds great, right?

Except my setup wasn't exactly cooperating.

I'm running Arch-based Linux with Wayland on a laptop with hybrid graphics:

  • Intel Raptor Lake UHD integrated graphics
  • NVIDIA RTX 4090 Laptop GPU

And getting Chrome, Vulkan, NVIDIA, and Wayland to play nicely together was an absolute pain.

There are several layers involved. Your GPU drivers need to work, Vulkan needs to find the right device, Chrome needs to use the right graphics backend, and WebGPU needs to initialize successfully.

And just because one of those things works doesn't mean the next one will.

I spent a lot of time troubleshooting different configurations before I finally had something reliable enough to use regularly.

The solution that worked for me

Eventually, I ended up with a Bash script that launches a separate Chrome instance configured specifically for WebGPU.

Here's the script I recovered:

#!/usr/bin/env bash

# Launch Google Chrome with NVIDIA PRIME offload + Vulkan + WebGPU on X11.
# Dedicated separate profile so it can run alongside normal Chrome.

set -euo pipefail

CHROME_PROFILE_DIR="${HOME}/.config/chrome-webgpu-nvidia"

mkdir -p "$CHROME_PROFILE_DIR"

VK_LOADER_DRIVERS_SELECT='*nvidia*' \
__NV_PRIME_RENDER_OFFLOAD=1 \
__GLX_VENDOR_LIBRARY_NAME=nvidia \
__VK_LAYER_NV_optimus=NVIDIA_only \
google-chrome-stable \
  --user-data-dir="$CHROME_PROFILE_DIR" \
  --enable-unsafe-webgpu \
  --enable-features=Vulkan \
  --ozone-platform=x11 \
  "$@"

It's not particularly complicated to look at.

But getting to the point where I knew which settings to use was another story.

I also created a .desktop launcher for it, so now when I want to experiment with WebGPU, I can just open that version of Chrome without having to remember any of this.

Which, as we've established, is probably a good thing.

What all those settings actually do

1. Getting Chrome to use the NVIDIA GPU

My laptop has two GPUs. There's the integrated Intel GPU and the dedicated NVIDIA GPU.

With hybrid graphics, applications don't necessarily use the GPU you'd expect.

That's a problem when you're trying to run models on your RTX 4090 and your browser decides the integrated GPU looks perfectly adequate.

So my script sets four environment variables:

VK_LOADER_DRIVERS_SELECT='*nvidia*'
__NV_PRIME_RENDER_OFFLOAD=1
__GLX_VENDOR_LIBRARY_NAME=nvidia
__VK_LAYER_NV_optimus=NVIDIA_only

Here's what they're for:

  • VK_LOADER_DRIVERS_SELECT filters the Vulkan driver manifests so that the NVIDIA driver is selected.
  • __NV_PRIME_RENDER_OFFLOAD=1 enables NVIDIA PRIME render offloading.
  • __GLX_VENDOR_LIBRARY_NAME=nvidia selects NVIDIA for GLX vendor dispatch.
  • __VK_LAYER_NV_optimus=NVIDIA_only tells NVIDIA's Optimus Vulkan layer to expose only the NVIDIA GPU.

Not all four variables necessarily matter for every application or graphics path, but this combination was part of my working configuration.

The important thing was making sure Chrome could actually access and use the GPU I wanted.

2. Making Wayland cooperate by... not using native Wayland

This one still makes me laugh.

I'm running a Wayland desktop, but my working Chrome launcher includes:

--ozone-platform=x11

That tells Chrome to use its X11 backend, which runs through XWayland inside my Wayland session.

At the time, I was running into problems getting Vulkan and Chrome's native Wayland backend to cooperate with NVIDIA.

Running Chrome through XWayland was the workaround that finally worked for my setup.

So after all that effort to get things running properly under Wayland, part of my solution was essentially telling Chrome to pretend it was running under X11.

Sometimes the practical solution isn't the elegant one.

It's the one that actually works.

3. Giving Chrome its own profile

This was one of the more useful discoveries.

--user-data-dir="$CHROME_PROFILE_DIR"

Chrome normally reuses an existing browser instance when you try to launch it again with the same profile.

So if Chrome is already open and you try launching another window with different GPU flags, you might discover that your new settings aren't actually being applied.

Using a separate profile directory gives my WebGPU launcher its own Chrome process and GPU configuration.

That also means I can keep my regular browser open while running a separate instance for development.

No need to mess with my normal browsing setup every time I want to test something.

4. Enabling Vulkan and WebGPU

Finally, these two flags:

--enable-unsafe-webgpu
--enable-features=Vulkan

The first enables experimental WebGPU support and bypasses certain GPU restrictions.

The second enables Chromium's Vulkan graphics feature.

There's an important distinction here: enabling Vulkan in Chrome doesn't necessarily guarantee that WebGPU itself is using Vulkan through Dawn, Chromium's WebGPU implementation.

The exact behavior depends on your Chromium version, platform, and graphics configuration.

Also, --enable-unsafe-webgpu is intended for development and testing. It's not something I'd recommend casually enabling in your everyday browser.

A note about newer Chrome versions: WebGPU support on Linux has been improving, so you might not need this exact configuration anymore. In particular, newer releases have expanded support for Intel and NVIDIA hardware. Check your current browser and driver support before copying every flag into your own setup.

How to check whether it's actually working

After launching Chrome with the script, open:

chrome://gpu

Look at the Graphics Feature Status section.

Ideally, you want to see hardware acceleration enabled for WebGPU and Vulkan rather than software fallbacks.

It's also worth checking the GPU and driver information to make sure Chrome is using the NVIDIA device instead of Intel or a software renderer like SwiftShader.

But don't stop there.

Being able to see WebGPU listed as hardware accelerated doesn't guarantee your actual application will run correctly.

Try running a real WebGPU sample or the model you're planning to use.

I've learned this the hard way more than once.

For example, while building my recent Mimu note-taking app, Safari on my iPhone reported that WebGPU was available. But attempting to initialize the Whisper model with WebGPU caused the tab to crash and reload.

The WASM version worked fine.

And for that particular small model, WASM was fast enough that using WebGPU wasn't worth the trouble anyway.

That was another useful reminder that the theoretically faster option isn't always the best one.

And then I forgot where I put everything

So here's where this whole thing comes full circle.

Recently, I've started keeping detailed build logs for my projects.

Not just what I built, but what broke, what I tried, why I made certain decisions, and what I'd do differently if I approached the same problem again.

Writing more on DEV has actually encouraged this habit. Thinking about what I might eventually write makes me pay more attention to what I'm doing while I'm building.

And I've already found myself going back through my notes and reconsidering decisions I made just a day or two earlier.

Which got me thinking about all those earlier experiences with WebGPU.

I wished I'd documented them better.

Turns out, I had.

I just couldn't remember doing it.

My AI agent found the original launcher in:

~/.local/bin/chrome-webgpu-nvidia

The desktop entry was in:

~/.local/share/applications/

And the documentation and additional copies were sitting in my PINKPIXEL/RESOURCES directory.

In two different folders.

I had already done everything I was wishing past me had done.

I just hadn't done a particularly good job of making that information easy to find again.

Which is even funnier considering I'm currently building an app designed to help people capture, organize, and remember things.

Apparently, I really do need it.

What I learned from all this

The technical lesson here is that getting WebGPU working on Linux can involve more than just enabling a browser flag, especially with hybrid graphics.

Depending on your hardware and software versions, you may need to pay attention to which GPU is being selected, which graphics backend Chrome is using, and whether your application is actually getting hardware acceleration.

But I think the bigger lesson for me has less to do with WebGPU.

I've built a lot of things over the years. I've solved problems, experimented with technologies, and figured out workarounds that took far more effort than I expected.

And then I moved on to the next interesting thing.

I didn't always stop to think about what I'd learned or how useful that experience might be later.

That's something I've been trying to change.

Keeping build logs has made me more thoughtful about the decisions I'm making, and writing about my experiences has encouraged me to look at them more closely.

Sometimes that means discovering a better way to approach something.

Sometimes it means remembering a useful technique.

And sometimes it means finding out that I already solved a problem, documented it, backed it up twice, and completely forgot about the whole thing.

At least now I know where my WebGPU script is.

For the moment, anyway.

articles.title: PHP2Shell, explained: the two critical PHP bugs every team needs to patch
articles.description: On October 21, 2026, PHP shipped an emergency security release for two critical vulnerabilities in...
articles.body_html:
On October 21, 2026, PHP shipped an emergency security release for two critical vulnerabilities in the PHP runtime itself. The pair is being called PHP2Shell:

  • CVE-2026-109618
  • CVE-2026-109619

Both have a 9.2 Critical CVSS score. Both can expose vulnerable PHP services to unauthenticated remote code execution and memory disclosure. And neither one is fixed by updating Laravel, WordPress, Symfony, a Composer package, or your application code.

This is the important part:

The vulnerable thing is the PHP interpreter that runs your application.

So yes, the meme is funny. The patch window is not.

First: should you be worried?

You should move this to the top of the queue if you run PHP on an internet-facing service and your runtime is any version from PHP 5.4 through PHP 8.5.11.

That includes more than the obvious php-fpm server in a VM:

  • PHP-FPM behind Nginx or Apache
  • Apache mod_php
  • WordPress, Drupal, Magento, Moodle, and other PHP-based products
  • Docker images built from php:* base images
  • Kubernetes workloads
  • queue workers and scheduled jobs
  • application images deployed to Cloud Run, ECS, App Engine Flexible, or similar platforms
  • vendor software that silently bundles its own PHP runtime

This is why security incidents around language runtimes are awkward: everyone knows where the repository is, but fewer teams can answer which PHP binary is actually serving production traffic right now?

What actually happened?

PHP receives a request, allocates memory, builds internal structures, runs your code, cleans everything up, and does it again for the next request. Most of the time, none of this is visible to an application developer. It should not be visible.

PHP2Shell lives in the parts of that lifecycle you only notice when something has already gone wrong: out-of-memory handling, cleanup, freed memory, and reused workers.

Think of a restaurant kitchen.

Normally, an order comes in, a tray is prepared, food is served, the tray is cleaned, and the next order starts with an empty tray. These vulnerabilities are different flavours of the kitchen being interrupted mid-cleanup—and the next order being served from a tray the system thought was safe, but was not.

That is a deliberately simplified analogy. The practical consequence is not: “your page crashes.” The reported impact is much worse: an unauthenticated attacker may be able to manipulate the runtime into leaking memory or executing code in the PHP process.

The two CVEs, in human language

CVE The technical shape The plain-English version Why defenders care
CVE-2026-109618 During an out-of-memory condition, PHP can be interrupted while request data is only partially initialized. Subsequent cleanup can treat that invalid state as valid. The runtime gets interrupted while setting up the request, then later cleans up a half-built object as if it were complete. The failure path can become an attacker-controlled path.
CVE-2026-109619 Request-owned state can remain reachable after its backing memory has been freed. A later request on the same worker can use stale state before normal initialization resets it. One request leaves behind a poisonous sticky note; the next request on the same worker reads it before the desk is reset. Long-lived, reused PHP workers make cross-request state especially relevant.

The research and vendor advisories use precise memory-management language because the details matter for exploitability. You do not need to reproduce that research to respond safely. The operational conclusion is already clear: update the runtime, restart/redeploy every worker that might still have the old binary or old in-memory state, and verify the version that is actually live.

Why “we use a framework” is not the answer

Framework updates are valuable. They just solve a different class of problem.

A typical framework vulnerability might be triggered by a route, a package feature, an insecure deserialization path, or an app-level configuration choice. With PHP2Shell, the issue is underneath that stack:

Your application
↓
Laravel / WordPress / Symfony / custom code
↓
Composer dependencies
↓
PHP runtime   ← the vulnerable layer
↓
OS or container image

You can have pristine dependencies, a clean SAST report, and still be running an affected PHP interpreter. That is why the right opening question is not “Which repo uses PHP?” It is “Which live workloads execute PHP?”

Which versions are affected—and what fixes them?

The disclosed affected range is PHP 5.4 through PHP 8.5.11.

The initial fixed upstream releases are:

Supported branch Fixed release
PHP 8.5 8.5.12
PHP 8.4 8.4.27
PHP 8.3 8.3.36
PHP 8.2 8.2.35

PHP 8.1 and older are end of life and are not receiving an upstream fix. If you are on one of those branches, the decision is not “which patch do we wait for?” It is “which supported PHP branch can we upgrade to safely and quickly?”

One nuance for distro users: a Linux distribution can backport a security patch while retaining a different-looking upstream version string. Follow your distribution’s security advisory and package changelog, then verify the installed package. For custom builds and official PHP images, move to a fixed upstream release.

The container trap: patching the host may change nothing

This is the moment where many incident checklists quietly fail.

Imagine a host running the latest system PHP package. Great. But your production app is deployed as this:

FROM php:8.3-fpm
COPY . /var/www/html

The PHP process serving requests came from the image, not from the host package manager. Updating the host does not alter the PHP binary already baked into that image.

The real fix path is:

update base image or PHP package
→ rebuild image
→ push a new immutable digest
→ redeploy every workload
→ verify the running container

The same rule applies to queue workers, cron jobs, admin jobs, and one-off worker deployments. They often have a separate Dockerfile, release pipeline, or autoscaling pool.

“The build succeeded” is not the final check. “The running workload uses the patched runtime” is.

A calm, practical response plan

1. Find every runtime

Start by checking what a machine or container is running:

php -v
php --ini

For container fleets, find images that contain PHP, then inspect the deployed digest in your orchestration platform. Search your CI definitions too: the old base image may be pinned in a reusable workflow rather than in the application repository.

Do not forget:

  • background queues
  • scheduled jobs
  • worker pools
  • maintenance scripts
  • staging and pre-production environments that hold production-like data
  • marketplace or vendor products with bundled PHP

2. Patch the runtime

Update to the fixed release for your supported branch—or to a vendor-confirmed package that contains the backported fix. For source builds, use the fixed upstream release. For containers, rebuild from a fixed base image or package set.

3. Restart or redeploy the processes

Installing a package is only half a fix if PHP-FPM or Apache is still running an old process in memory. Restart the relevant service. In container platforms, deploy fresh tasks/pods/instances from the patched image.

This matters especially for a bug involving request-owned state and reused workers: stale, running processes are not where you want to gamble on “probably fine.”

4. Verify the live environment

Check the runtime version from a newly started process, not just from your laptop or CI log:

php -v

For containers, also verify the new image digest is the one your deployment actually pulled. An autoscaler can keep old replicas alive longer than expected; an image tag can be reused; a rollout can partially fail. Those are normal operational problems. They are also how a completed patch turns into an incomplete remediation.

5. Monitor and investigate, without turning this into panic theatre

The FBI’s public guidance recommends prioritizing internet-facing systems, watching for suspicious PHP processes launching command shells or downloading files, and preserving relevant logs if compromise indicators appear. Qualys also reported that Cloudflare had observed attack traffic, which is a good reason to treat external exposure as urgent rather than theoretical.

Useful places to review:

  • web-server access and error logs
  • PHP-FPM / Apache error logs
  • process-execution telemetry from affected hosts and containers
  • WAF and load-balancer events
  • application error-rate and restart telemetry
  • image-scanner results after the rebuild

Unexpected 5xx spikes, repeated process crashes, large unusual request bodies, unexpected shell processes, or unexplained downloads deserve incident-response attention. They are signals to investigate—not proof by themselves that the CVE was exploited.

“Can a WAF save us?”

A WAF can buy time. It cannot patch a vulnerable interpreter.

Cloud guidance for this incident recommends using managed WAF protections and being careful about oversized request bodies while patching. That is reasonable defence in depth, especially for public applications. Roll new rules out in preview/canary mode where feasible, look for application-specific false positives, then enforce them.

But do not let a temporary rule become a reason to defer the update. A rule protects only the traffic it sees, only the shapes it recognizes, and only the applications placed behind it. The runtime update is the remediation.

The posts people are sharing on X

These are real posts published after the disclosure. They are included here because they add useful operational perspective—not because social media is a source of truth. The PHP security advisory and your platform/vendor guidance should drive the actual patch plan.

FBI Cyber Division: treat exposed installations as urgent

Qualys: patch, restart workers, and verify the runtime

Datadog: check versions across the organization

The things teams will get wrong this week

“We updated WordPress, so we are safe.”

Maybe you are safer from a WordPress vulnerability. That is not the same as replacing the PHP binary that runs WordPress.

“We upgraded the server package.”

Excellent—unless the service runs inside a container, an immutable image, a separate worker pool, or a vendor distribution with its own runtime.

“Our scanner says the repository is clean.”

Source scanning does not prove the running infrastructure has the right runtime. Scan the image, check the deployed digest, and verify the live process.

“We are on PHP 8.1, but it is stable.”

Stable is not supported. There is no upstream security release for PHP 8.1 or older here. Upgrade planning just became incident response work.

“We put a WAF rule in front of it.”

Good temporary mitigation. Still not a patch.

Your incident checklist

  • [ ] Identify every production, worker, and scheduled workload that executes PHP.
  • [ ] Confirm whether its PHP runtime is in the affected range.
  • [ ] Update to PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, 8.2.35, or a vendor-confirmed patched build.
  • [ ] Upgrade PHP 8.1 and older to a supported branch.
  • [ ] Rebuild custom images without relying on a stale cache.
  • [ ] Redeploy every workload and restart long-lived PHP processes.
  • [ ] Verify the live runtime version and image digest.
  • [ ] Apply temporary WAF/edge controls while rollout completes.
  • [ ] Review security telemetry and preserve evidence if compromise indicators appear.
  • [ ] Record which environments are verified and which still need work.

The takeaway

PHP is a widely deployed runtime having a serious emergency patch day.

The less funny takeaway is that runtime upgrades cannot live forever in a low-priority maintenance bucket. The moment a core vulnerability lands, the teams that respond well are the ones that already know:

  1. where their runtimes are,
  2. how their images are built,
  3. how to roll out a change everywhere, and
  4. how to prove that the change reached production.

Patch it. Redeploy it. Verify it.

References

  • PHP’s October 21 security announcement
  • PHP advisory for CVE-2026-109618
  • PHP advisory for CVE-2026-109619
  • Google Cloud’s remediation guidance

Have you checked your worker images yet, or only the web servers?

It has this special thing about it... it helps the newer voices get discovered. Its algorithm is designed like that!!

More than 5 posts are getting indexed, and others will be there soon... lol.

That increases the reach of the platform and the posts of new voices.

So, I think all the algorithms, user engagement emails, notifications, and main features are almost done.

I think I just need a little UI improvement now! And then 2–3 days of testing!

And in UI improvements, I need to fix the sidebars, and a few buttons are very close to each other. I need to fix those, and... all set!

Finally, I feel like I'm at the moment where it's just done!

But idk how this just goes on. I need to add this... just this much, this much more... hmm... more and more...

But I think this is enough. I just need UI improvements now, and that's it for now!

Further, I got 12 users now, and 60 posts on Crowdwide are completed. Ik most of them are devlogs, but still, I count this as part of building, too. I also posted my old artwork there—a paper flower built by me:

https://www.crowdwide.run.place/posts/6ad739d24eabf9bab7720410

I will post things on it... some interesting things, and maybe on different topics...

I don't want its feed to get dead!

And the number of communities is still the same!

There's no major growth in the number of users. I found mostly old users there.

So, I will try to make a few more posts on different topics and try to continue until it gets its first 100 users.

Ik it may take a lot of time, but I will try this.

Not afraid of failing or just ending up with another ONLY showcase for my profile!

articles.title: Enshittification Accounting: Budgeting for Migrations and Switching
articles.description: (Editorial note: I originally published this over on the Hit Subscribe blog.)  I received this email...
articles.body_html:
(Editorial note: I originally published this over on the Hit Subscribe blog.)

I received this email from Atlassian, who, a while back, purchased one of my most cherished B2B tools: Loom.  I use Loom constantly, and I've historically loved it.  But now, obviously, it's time to move on.

That might seem like a dramatic overreaction to the email, or at least a little glib.  $8 to $15 per month (or $24 to $45 for the number of seats I think we have) is at most a minor annoyance for a business that wants to keep using a valuable tool.  So what gives?

Well, what gives is that I'm not reacting to the price -- I'm reacting to the extraction pattern.  I'm reacting to the inevitable fate of Loom.  And I'm reacting in a predictable enough way that I realized that I could schedule my reaction to enshittification.  In fact, I could even budget for it, and I'm going to riff on that idea in this post.

The Fate of Loom: Funnel Asset for Enterprise Sales

Let me explain the Loom situation in a bit more detail to justify why I think switching away from it is a simple, pragmatic inevitability.  After all, I've been down this road with another formerly-beloved, and largely-abandoned tool: Trello.  Atlassian has acquired both tools.

Atlassian's bread and butter is selling project management tools into the enterprise. Trello and Loom, on the other hand, have historically had much wider user bases, so there is some overlap, but not a ton.  At least not initially.

Functionally speaking, an enterprise using Jira and Confluence is a much better, more important customer than a freelancer's freemium interaction with Trello for keeping track of a todo list.  So much so that I would argue Trello and Loom are more valuable to Atlassian as marketing assets for their core business than they are as standalone businesses in their own right.  And everything about the behavior of these tools, post-acquisition, supports that hypothesis.

From here, I don't think it's a huge leap to say that Trello and Loom users whose behavior indicates they're a qualified lead for the core business are more interesting to Atlassian than other users.  And I also don't think it's a leap to say that the feature roadmap, support behavior, and pricing of these businesses will, and from their perspective, should, accentuate that distinction.   Funnel the qualified leads in and gently invite the unqualified ones, like Hit Subscribe, to piss off.

Forcing the Non-Qualified Leads off the Platform

I imagine a lot of former Trello users can relate to what I'm about to say.  When I started using Trello, you logged into Trello and used it.  But post-acquisition, Atlassian rolled out some kind of unified login experience that gradually forced you to create an Atlassian account. The result is a confusing coexistence of legacy and current credentials that occasionally turns logging into Trello into an infuriating 10-minute side quest.

I'm looking forward to that same mildly infuriating experience now with Loom, sooner or later.  If I were a Jira user, this would likely be pretty convenient -- hey, I'm just magically auth-ed into these tools now!  As a non-Jira user, it's awful.  So if you go back and read the email I received from Atlassian, here's how it actually lands with me.

Good news, Loom user!  Now that you're involuntarily part of the Atlassian ecosystem, not only will things be generally worse and your login experience Kafkaesque, but it's twice as expensive!  Don't like it?  Sucks to be you!

You might say I'm being overly cynical, and I can admit that I'm frustrated in what I see to be the inevitable nerfing of one of my favorite B2B tools, but even the most benign and charitable read of this has the price doubling, the product roadmap radically altered, and new stuff I don't want.  So in the blink of an acquisition, Loom became more expensive and less useful for my business.

Whether you refer to this as "enshittification" or "extracting value out of locked in users," however, I'd say planning for and around it can look the same.  And there are levers to pull, which is what I'll discuss shortly.

But to close the loop on whether I was overreacting to the email or not, I was not.  That's because my worry isn't the price increase or the email itself.  Instead, the email served as a reminder that, since I'm not an enterprise user, the company who owns Loom no longer cares about having me as a Loom customer.  And that's an unsustainable situation in which to be a customer.

Thinking Timelines

Elided from the screenshot above, and to Atlassian's credit, they're giving me plenty of notice.  The price increase doesn't actually hit for 7 months, which is plenty of time to plan around a relatively nominal change in raw dollars.

 

You can also, if you're interested, go read their rationale for the price increase.  It's a mix of every business's "we built a bunch of Slopware nobody asked for and someone has to pay for that", a few genuine value-adds from the historical roadmap, and a bunch of Confluence and Jira integration that would only appeal to qualified leads using Loom.

So what you have here is a pretty classic acquisition and extraction move, laid out over a fairly gradual timeline.  Atlassian seems even more benign when you consider that they acquired Loom in late 2023 and have, other than the janky login stuff, left the thing pretty much alone and left me to remain as a happy user.

However, I could have foreseen and predicted the extraction, increases, and altered feature roadmap all the way back in 2023.  And I could have planned for it.

And, in fact, I'm doing just that with Airtable.  Airtable was recently acquired by a company famous for extracting hard and fast (layoffs, eliminating free tiers, raising rates, etc).  In the three weeks following that announcement, I actually completely migrated Osiris away from using Airtable as a combo-GUI/backend, removing the only critical dependency we have there.  We'll plan to take a more measured approach to the rest of our collaboration but are hoping to be Airtable-free by the time the deal goes through.

Enshittification Mechanics

I don't want to belabor the point here, but it's worth understanding why acquisitions give rise to this sort of thing.  You can read in detail Cory Doctorow's take on enshittification and read more about the mechanics of it in general.  But that's a description inextricable from social commentary.

To give it a more neutral take, it's simply the idea of extracting more value (money) out of existing assets.  In and of itself, there's nothing inherently wrong with that. It's what a freelancer does after realizing they're "under-charging" and that clients would pay more.  Raise rates for the same deliverable, extract value via leverage.

Where things start to become much grayer is where tactics around doing that start to involve taking advantage of (or creating) massive switching costs and the use of dark patterns.  I'm not going to weigh in on this too much, since this post isn't about whether this should happen, but about sharing an idea for how to handle it.

So for our purposes here, understand that acquisitions are usually followed by the acquiring party engaging in value extraction -- grabbing money the original company was leaving on the table.

And you should also understand two more things about extraction:

  1. It will work on you in direct proportion to how locked in you are, and how expensive it would be for you to pursue an alternative approach.
  2. The acquiring party often has to raise rates because the purpose of an early stage company in venture-land is to gain users, not to be profitable.  So startups will often offer unsustainably low prices to acquire users (think Uber) knowing that eventually they, or an acquirer will have to pay the piper.  tl;dr: pre-extraction offerings are usually unsustainably cheap.

Being Anti-Extractable

With this in mind, let's think about what it would look like to build a business that was immune to, or at least very resistant to extraction/enshittification.  If your goal were to deal with this as little as possible, how would you handle it?

The most naive suggestion would be "don't do business with startups."  And while I don't actually recommend that rule, its extreme formulation carries an interesting lesson.  When you're doing business with startups, you need to be aware that the offer is likely too good to be long-term true, and also that there will eventually be a piper coming to collect his pay.

Another important aspect of avoiding this fate is to look at each SaaS subscription on your expense sheet and think about what you would do if it 2x-ed or 10x-ed its price.  If the answer is "we'd be doomed," that's no good.  If the answer is "meh, we actually did a trial with one of their competitors a few months ago, so no biggie," you're in better shape.

So an anti-extractable business looks heuristically like this:

  1. Aware of where in the extraction lifecycle its vendors are.
  2. Aware of the magnitude and complexity of its dependencies.
  3. Able to switch nimbly to alternatives in the face of an extraction power play.
  4. Minimally dependent on vendors in danger of becoming extraction farms.

How do you become a company like this?  Well, I have an interesting hypothesis that might make it easier than it sounds with a relatively simple accounting trick.

Enshittification Accounting: The Mechanics

Here's how I could see this working.  You price SaaS and services based not on their introductory discount or current rate, but on an estimate what you think the eventual market price would be.  This becomes your budget for that thing.

So, for instance, take my Loom subscription.  Back when I started paying for it, probably 5 years ago, I could have said, "$8 per month seems unsustainably cheap for this.  I imagine that for this to be profitable, it should really cost something like $30 per month."  (Ignore for the moment how one would arrive at that figure -- I'll get to that).  This means that my budget for video collaboration is $30 per month, per seat.

That also becomes what I pay, through a trick of accounting.

That's because I create a checking account, called, say, Enshittification Escrow.  And then I set up a monthly transfer from OpEx checking to Enshittification Escrow for $90 (I think we have 3 Loom seats), which means I'm "paying" the full, sustainable price for Loom.  I then also pay the $24 per month Loom bill out of the Enshittification Escrow account.  So I'm transferring $90 per month into this account, while paying $24 per month out of it, assuming Loom is my only enshittification candidate in the beginning.

The effect that this would create would be money pooling in the escrow account.  To be precise, after 60 months of this, I would have amassed $3,960 of surplus.  Now, imagine the impact of doing this across a variety of underpriced offerings.  For me, this would have included Airtable, Loom, ETL solutions, SEO tooling, API credits, and more.

The "Macro" Economics of Enshittification Escrow

To be clear, this is NOT primarily a savings play.  The goal isn't to trick yourself into saving money, which genuinely makes little sense for a business deploying capital in order to profit and grow.

Rather, it is primarily about creating optionality and a buffer for smooth operations.

To illustrate what I mean, let's swap out a trivial example like Loom in favor of something more complex, like Airtable.  Right now our Airtable bill runs around $100 per month.  But let's say that Bending Spoons sent an email saying "great news, we've 10x-ed your price in exchange for nothing you want!"  I'd have a few bad options, which is generally the goal with extraction plays.

  1. Pay $1,000 per month to avoid disrupting client collaboration.
  2. Try to foist some of the cost onto clients, annoying them.
  3. Scramble to implement some kind of migration plan.
  4. Haggle with them for some kind of special consideration.

But now let's say that I'd pooled $4K into my enshittification escrow account.  Suddenly things look rosier with my options:

  1. Kick the decision down the road a month or two, paying $1K out of the escrow in the meantime.
  2. Migrate methodically to a competitive offering with plenty of client notice.
  3. Give clients notice that an Airtable surcharge is coming, and migrate those who don't want to pay it.
  4. Hire a consultant to identify and migrate to a replacement.

The escrow account is designed to keep things running smoothly.  And it works because the entire idea of an extraction play is to ransom smoothness back to you at gunpoint.  The rainy-day fund removes the gun from the equation.

The Business Upsides

I had this idea on the way to the gym a few weeks ago and started the blog post.  As I've mulled it over since then, I think this approach would have a number of interesting and positive effects on a small business beyond just creating optionality in the face of extractive price increases or defeaturing.  It would create some potentially helpful incentives and natural signals.

(While I haven't read the book, I believe Michael Michalowicz pioneered the idea of strategic use of bank accounts as business optimization in his Profit First book and accounting.  So I'm drawing a bit of inspiration here from what I understand his approach to be).

1. Minimizes Excessive Business Dependencies

If I learned anything as a kid from "Just Say No" drug commercials in the 80s, it's that the first one is free, and then it's gonna cost ya.  Whether we're talking about drugs, free cheese samples at the grocery store, or introductory SaaS pricing, the world has learned to front-load benefits and delay real cost decisions on behalf of prospects everywhere.  Buy now, pay later.

From a business ownership perspective, this has ramifications beyond simply distorting your perception of cost-benefit.  It encourages you with minimal friction to sign up for something, start using it, realize some value.  It encourages dependency.  "Wow, this Loom thing is cool, let's take it for a whirl and see if clients like explainer videos."

It's a much less disruptive decision to simply not "take it for a whirl" than it is to decide to stop using it years later, with a whole bunch of clients that actively appreciate your Looms.

Low-friction adoption creates a glide path to problematic dependencies.  Introducing friction to the adoption process in the form of pricing and setting up account transfer increases the friction to creating those dependencies.

And crucially that is the moment where you ask yourself "is this really worth coming to rely on?"  The answer to that is probably "no" a lot more often than you assume.

2. Forces Honest Valuations of Vendor Offerings

Part and parcel with discouraging superfluous dependencies is the forced valuation of what a vendor is offering.  When you sign up for something, the question you're generally answering in the moment is "would I pay X for Y," where X is the current (often pre-enshittification) price.  Rarely are you asking the question "what's the most I would be willing to pay for Y?"

That latter amount is actually Y's value to you.  Anything less that you pay becomes a form of arbitrage, at least in the short term.

Think back to my earlier example of Loom, and the $30 figure I hand-waved at.  In order to take an educated guess at what something should cost, I'd have to do a bit of recon.  What do their competitors tend to charge?  What would it cost to DIY?  What is their cost?

Reasoning intentionally about the cost of something naturally forces you to grapple with what the service is actually worth to you.  That may not actually be the same thing as what it should cost, either.  So there's obviously some guess work and nuance happening here.

But the upside of what may seem like overthinking is that you are clear-eyed about what you would, and wouldn't, pay for something.  And further, you're clear about how likely, post-enshittification, it is that the offering will continue to sit in the window of acceptable cost for you.

With this discipline in place, you will always know, automatically, that you're paying what, or less than, something is worth to you.

3. A Bellwether for Expense Creep

And "automatically" is a great way to find yourself describing decisions about cost.  As your business grows and your dependencies grow, you won't be able to spend time constantly re-litigating your vendor arrangements after every minor price increase or scope change.

This brings me to another interesting property of this style of accounting.  The balance of your escrow account will actually tell you a lot about expense management at a glance.

If the balance is increasing, that means you have a favorable average relationship with your vendors.  You're consistently paying less than you'd be willing to pay.  You're, in aggregate, "getting a good deal".

If your account balance is high and you're breaking even or gradually declining, it might be time for an audit.  A balance decline means that enough rate increases and scope reductions have occurred that you're no longer getting a good deal, according to your own valuations.

Find the offenders and re-evaluate.  It could be as simple as raising the amount you put into the escrow account, if you value those vendors more.  Otherwise, flag them for replacement, plan a migration, and get back into a situation where the account balance grows.

4. A Specifically Scoped Lender

And, finally, a benefit that is more about finance than ops management.  Creating an escrow account designed to defray unexpected expenses means you're positioning yourself as a lender to your own business.

Over the course of time, if you have an escrow account that pools four or even five figures of cash, you can dip into it for temporary cash flow situations.  And, unlike a business line of credit or a credit card, you're not paying any interest on the loan.

That said, if you do this, I would advise treating it as a genuine loan.  If you don't track it and repay it (potentially with interest), you lose the aforementioned benefits and you also lose the cash you're attempting to build to stop vendors from extorting you over the cost of switching.

Use in Good Health (And Let Me Know!)

I'm mulling this over with Hit Subscribe, and seriously considering it for the LLC I have for a vacation rental property.  The only real downside and barrier is creating an additional checking account and the expense associated with it, if applicable.  (I don't think Chase charges me, so it's really just the hassle of setting it up.)  So I'll probably implement this at some point.

But if this sounds like a good idea to you -- if this triggers an aha! moment and you set it up -- please let me know.  I'd be genuinely curious to hear any tales of how this plays out in practice.

Vendors in general, and SaaS in particular, have, for better or worse, landed on enshittification as a mainstream tactic.  This means that your vendor pool is actively looking to conceal the nature of your spending and your dependencies from you.  Business finance in that world doesn't require "more diligence" about your subscriptions and contracts -- it requires a fundamentally different approach.

articles.title: The Hidden Bugs Behind Duplicate API Requests
articles.description: One click on "Place order." Two rows in the orders table, created 40 milliseconds apart, identical...
articles.body_html:
One click on "Place order." Two rows in the orders table, created 40 milliseconds apart, identical down to the last field.

Nothing in the frontend code looks wrong. The server logs show two requests, both returning 201. Whoever wrote the endpoint is fairly sure it only creates one order per call, and they're right. It was called twice.

"Duplicate request" is a symptom with at least six different causes, and the fixes don't overlap much. Some of these causes are harmless (React in development), some are annoying (a double-clicked button), and one is genuinely dangerous: a client that timed out and sent the request again, while the server had already done the work. This article goes through them roughly in the order I'd check them, and spends the most time on that last one, because it's the one that costs money.

Before you debug: is it really a duplicate?

Three things look like duplicates and aren't.

CORS preflight. A cross-origin request with a JSON Content-Type, an Authorization header, or a method like PUT makes the browser send an OPTIONS request first. In DevTools the URL appears twice. Look at the Method column. (MDN: CORS preflight)

Development-only behavior. If the doubles show up on your machine but not in production, go straight to the React section below.

A different caller. A service worker, browser extension, or second tab can send requests that resemble yours. The Initiator column in the Network tab points at the line that started each request.

Then do the single most useful thing: log a request ID on the server. One request on the server means you're misreading the client. Two means keep reading.

React runs your effect twice (on purpose) 

function Product({ id }) {
  const [product, setProduct] = useState(null);

  useEffect(() => {
    fetch(`/api/products/${id}`)
      .then(r => r.json())
      .then(setProduct);
  }, [id]);
}

Under <StrictMode> in development, this sends two requests on mount. In a production build it sends one.

That's deliberate. With Strict Mode on, React runs an extra setup, cleanup, setup cycle on each effect in development, to expose effects that don't clean up after themselves. The behavior arrived with React 18, and the surprise it caused is well documented in facebook/react #24502, where users asked for it to be explained better in the docs.

Removing Strict Mode makes the symptom disappear and leaves the bug. If an effect misbehaves when it runs twice, it will also misbehave when a user navigates away and back.

For reads, add a cleanup that cancels the request:

useEffect(() => {
  const controller = new AbortController();

  fetch(`/api/products/${id}`, { signal: controller.signal })
    .then(r => r.json())
    .then(setProduct)
    .catch(err => {
      if (err.name !== 'AbortError') setError(err);
    });

  return () => controller.abort();
}, [id]);

You'll still see two requests in the Network tab in development, but the first is cancelled and only the second can touch state. An AbortController is better than the common ignore flag here: as this DEV Community post points out, the flag discards the result but still lets the first request download its whole response.

Cancelling on the client does not undo anything the server already did. Which brings up the real question this section raises: what is the effect doing? A duplicate GET is noise. A duplicate POST fired from an effect means a non-idempotent action is tied to rendering. React's guidance is that effects exist to synchronize with external systems, and that you don't need an effect to handle a user event. Creating an order belongs in the click handler, where it runs once per click.

Race conditions: the stale response wins

Sometimes two different requests are in flight and the older one finishes last.

A search box fires on every keystroke. The user types "re", then "react". The request for "re" is slow, the one for "react" is quick. Results for "react" render, then results for "re" arrive and overwrite them. The page now shows results for a query that no longer matches the input.

Nothing was sent twice, and nothing here is React-specific. The UI depends on the order responses arrive instead of the order the user acted. The cleanup shown above fixes it, since React runs the previous effect's cleanup before the next effect. If you'd rather not cancel, the flag version works too:

useEffect(() => {
  let ignore = false;
  fetch(`/api/search?q=${encodeURIComponent(query)}`)
    .then(r => r.json())
    .then(data => { if (!ignore) setResults(data); });
  return () => { ignore = true; };
}, [query]);

Debouncing the input reduces how many requests you send. The cleanup makes sure the right one wins. They solve different problems, and a search box usually needs both.

The double click

A checkout button, an 800 ms API call, and a user who isn't sure the first click registered.

Disabling the button during submission is the obvious fix, with one catch. State updates don't apply synchronously inside the handler that sets them, so two clicks that land before React re-renders can both pass an if (submitting) check. A ref closes that gap:

function CheckoutButton() {
  const [submitting, setSubmitting] = useState(false);
  const inFlight = useRef(false);

  async function handleClick() {
    if (inFlight.current) return;   // the real lock
    inFlight.current = true;
    setSubmitting(true);            // the visual feedback
    try {
      await placeOrder();
    } finally {
      inFlight.current = false;
      setSubmitting(false);
    }
  }

  return (
    <button onClick={handleClick} disabled={submitting}>
      {submitting ? 'Placing order…' : 'Place order'}
    </button>
  );
}

This protects one component in one tab. A second tab, a mobile app, or a retry after a dropped connection walks right past it. Treat it as UI feedback, and keep the safety check on the server.

The same handler attached twice

If the server log shows two identical requests a few milliseconds apart and the button logic is fine, count the listeners.

// runs on every route change
function init() {
  document.querySelector('#save')
    .addEventListener('click', () => saveDraft());
}

addEventListener ignores a repeat registration only when the function reference and capture flag are the same. An inline arrow function is a new object every call, so after three route changes one click runs saveDraft() three times. (MDN: addEventListener)

The usual sources are SPA code that attaches listeners imperatively on every navigation, jQuery's .on() inside a function that runs on every partial render, and React effects that subscribe without returning a cleanup. A form with both onSubmit on the <form> and onClick on its submit button doing the same job produces the same symptom.

In Chrome DevTools, select the element and open the Event Listeners panel. Two click entries where you expected one is your answer.

Retries: duplicates made by code that's trying to help

This is the case worth slowing down for.

You send a POST /orders. Ten seconds pass. Your client times out. Here is everything you know at that moment: you did not receive a response. Here is what you don't know:

  1. The request never reached the server.
  2. The server processed it, and the response was lost on the way back.
  3. The server is still working on it.

From the client these three look identical. If you retry in case 2 or 3, the operation runs twice.

HTTP has vocabulary for this. RFC 9110, section 9.2.2 defines idempotent methods: GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, TRACE, PUT and DELETE, where repeating the request has the same intended effect as sending it once. POST isn't in that set, and neither is PATCH in general. The RFC's error-handling section also notes that some requests can be automatically retried after a connection failure, pointing to section 9.2.2 for which ones. Secondary write-ups summarize the rule as: don't automatically retry a non-idempotent request unless you know it's effectively idempotent or can tell the original was never applied (ApyHub, a DEV Community post on safe failover).

Check what your client library does by default

Retry behavior varies by library and version, so read your client's documentation instead of assuming. One public example: a GitLab client-library change (merge request 2945) added an option to restrict retries to idempotent methods, because its default check retried any method on a 5xx response, which could duplicate a side effect the server had already applied. That's one project's default, but it shows how the problem hides: nobody wrote a retry for POST /orders; a generic retry policy did.

Retries multiply across layers

If the browser code retries 3 times, the API gateway retries 3 times, and the service retries its database call 3 times, one click can become 27 attempts at the bottom. Amazon's Builders' Library article on timeouts, retries and backoff with jitter makes this point about stacked retries, and also calls retries "selfish": each one spends more of the server's time to improve the caller's odds. Its recommendations are timeouts based on downstream latency, capped exponential backoff, jitter so clients don't all retry in lockstep, and limiting retries (the AWS SDK has used a token bucket for this since 2016).

Infrastructure retries too. Reverse proxies can pass a failed request to another upstream. For example, nginx's proxy_next_upstream documents that non-idempotent requests aren't passed on by default unless you opt in with non_idempotent. Read the equivalent setting for whatever sits in front of your app, and check access logs on every hop.

A retry helper that actually retries HTTP failures

One trap when writing your own: fetch() resolves successfully even when the server answers 503. A try/catch around it never sees the failure. You have to look at the status yourself.

class HttpError extends Error {
  constructor(res) {
    super(`HTTP ${res.status}`);
    this.status = res.status;
  }
}

const RETRYABLE_STATUS = new Set([408, 429, 500, 502, 503, 504]);

function isRetryable(err) {
  if (err.name === 'AbortError') return false;
  if (err instanceof HttpError) return RETRYABLE_STATUS.has(err.status);
  return err instanceof TypeError; // fetch rejects with TypeError on network failure
}

async function withRetry(fn, { retries = 4, baseMs = 200, capMs = 5000 } = {}) {
  for (let attempt = 0; ; attempt++) {
    try {
      return await fn();
    } catch (err) {
      if (attempt >= retries || !isRetryable(err)) throw err;
      const ceiling = Math.min(capMs, baseMs * 2 ** attempt);
      const delay = Math.random() * ceiling;          // full jitter
      await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, delay));
    }
  }
}

// usage
const res = await withRetry(async () => {
  const r = await fetch('/api/orders', { method: 'POST', /* ... */ });
  if (!r.ok) throw new HttpError(r);
  return r;
});

I ran this helper against a stub that returns 503 twice and then 201: it made three attempts and returned the 201. A 400 was thrown after one attempt, as intended. A production version should also honor a Retry-After header when the server sends one.

Retrying a POST with this helper is only safe if the server can recognize the repeat. That's the next section.

Making the server safe to call twice

Everything above reduces how often a duplicate arrives. None of it can remove the three-way ambiguity after a timeout, because the network is allowed to lose a response. For operations that must not happen twice, the main defense is an idempotency key: the client generates a unique key per logical operation, the server records it with the result, and a repeat with the same key returns the stored result instead of doing the work again.

Stripe's API is the best-known example. Their documentation says the idempotency layer saves the status code and body of the first request for a key, whether it succeeded or failed, and returns that for later requests with the same key. Keys can be up to 255 characters, and reusing a key with different parameters produces an error. GET and DELETE don't take keys because they're idempotent by definition.

There's also a standards effort: the IETF HTTPAPI working group's Idempotency-Key HTTP header field draft. As of the version I read (draft-07, October 2025), it's an active Internet-Draft, not an RFC, so details may change.

Client: create the key once, reuse it on every retry 

// Create it when the user's intent is created (page load, checkout start),
// never inside the retry loop.
const idempotencyKey = crypto.randomUUID();

await withRetry(async () => {
  const r = await fetch('/api/orders', {
    method: 'POST',
    headers: {
      'Content-Type': 'application/json',
      'Idempotency-Key': idempotencyKey,
    },
    body: JSON.stringify(order),
  });
  if (!r.ok) throw new HttpError(r);
  return r;
});

A new key per attempt defeats the whole mechanism.

Server: let the database arbitrate

The sketch below uses Express and PostgreSQL. It's an illustration of the pattern: I haven't run the SQL against a live database, so test it in your own stack, including the concurrent case.

CREATE TABLE idempotency_keys (
  key           text PRIMARY KEY,
  request_hash  text NOT NULL,
  response_code int  NOT NULL,
  response_body jsonb NOT NULL,
  created_at    timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

// Same payload in a different key order must hash the same.
function canonicalize(v) {
  if (Array.isArray(v)) return v.map(canonicalize);
  if (v && typeof v === 'object') {
    return Object.fromEntries(
      Object.keys(v).sort().map(k => [k, canonicalize(v[k])])
    );
  }
  return v;
}

app.post('/api/orders', async (req, res) => {
  const key = req.get('Idempotency-Key');
  if (!key) return res.status(400).json({ error: 'Idempotency-Key required' });

  const hash = sha256(JSON.stringify(canonicalize(req.body)));
  const client = await pool.connect();

  try {
    await client.query('BEGIN');

    // Claim the key. The PRIMARY KEY decides who wins a race.
    const claim = await client.query(
      `INSERT INTO idempotency_keys (key, request_hash, response_code, response_body)
       VALUES ($1, $2, 0, '{}')
       ON CONFLICT (key) DO NOTHING
       RETURNING key`,
      [key, hash]
    );

    if (claim.rowCount === 0) {
      await client.query('ROLLBACK');
      const { rows: [saved] } = await pool.query(
        'SELECT request_hash, response_code, response_body FROM idempotency_keys WHERE key = $1',
        [key]
      );
      if (!saved) return res.status(409).set('Retry-After', '1').end(); // first attempt rolled back
      if (saved.request_hash !== hash) {
        return res.status(422).json({ error: 'Key reused with a different payload' });
      }
      return res.status(saved.response_code).json(saved.response_body);
    }

    // We own the key. Do the work, in the same transaction.
    const order = await createOrder(client, req.body);
    const body = { id: order.id };

    await client.query(
      `UPDATE idempotency_keys SET response_code = 201, response_body = $2 WHERE key = $1`,
      [key, body]
    );
    await client.query('COMMIT');
    return res.status(201).json(body);
  } catch (err) {
    await client.query('ROLLBACK').catch(() => {});
    throw err;
  } finally {
    client.release();
  }
});

Three design points are worth spelling out.

Why INSERT ... ON CONFLICT and not "check, then insert." A SELECT followed by an INSERT has a gap, and two simultaneous requests can both pass the check. Letting a unique constraint decide closes the gap. As I understand PostgreSQL's behavior, a second insert of the same key blocks until the first transaction commits or rolls back, which is why the example doesn't need an in_progress state. Verify that against your isolation level and driver.

Why one transaction. Creating the order and recording the key together means a crash can't leave an order without a key, or a key without an order. This only works when both writes live in the same database. Once the operation involves something outside that transaction (a payment provider, a message queue, an email), the guarantee stops at the transaction boundary. For those, pass a key derived from yours to the provider's own idempotency mechanism, and consider an explicit in_progress state with a defined policy for concurrent callers, such as 409 with Retry-After.

Why canonicalize before hashing. JSON.stringify preserves key order, so {a:1,b:2} and {b:2,a:1} hash differently even though they mean the same thing. Without canonicalization, a legitimate retry from a different serializer gets rejected as "key reused with a different payload."

When a simpler rule is enough

If the domain gives you natural uniqueness, such as one open order per (user_id, cart_id), a unique constraint can reject the duplicate without any key table. Idempotency keys are the more general tool, and constraints are the cheaper one when they fit.

Idempotency isn't the only defense either. Uniqueness constraints, transactional design and operation-specific checks all contribute. What an idempotency key gives you that they don't is a consistent answer to the retry: the same response, not an error saying "already exists."

A checklist for the next time you see doubles

  1. Is one of them an OPTIONS preflight?
  2. Does it happen in a production build? If not, check Strict Mode and effect cleanups.
  3. What does the Initiator column say about each request?
  4. How many listeners does the element have?
  5. Does the server log show one request or two? Log a request ID.
  6. Are the two requests identical, or do query strings differ? Different ones suggest a race or dependency-array bug, not a retry.
  7. How far apart are the timestamps? Milliseconds points at a double-click or double-mount. Seconds points at a timeout and retry.
  8. Which layers retry? Browser code, client library, gateway, load balancer, service client, job queue.
  9. Can this endpoint safely run twice? If not, fix that first.

The first eight steps tell you why a duplicate happened. The ninth decides whether it matters.

articles.title: I Built an Agent Skill That Tests Your App Like Four First-Time Users
articles.description: Four simulated first-time users, one simple audit workflow, and a copy-paste prompt to try it on your app.
articles.body_html:
When you're building an app, you already know where every button leads and what the user is supposed to do next.

Your first-time visitors don't.

That's why I built First User Audit — an open-source Agent Skill that helps coding agents explore your application from four different first-time-user perspectives.

It focuses on one question:

Can someone reach the first useful result without getting stuck?

Four perspectives, one app

The skill uses four simulated user behaviors:

  • Impatient — Skims the page, clicks the obvious button, and quickly gives up when things get confusing.
  • Skeptic — Checks pricing, privacy, and terms before trusting the product.
  • Mobile — Explores the experience at a 375px viewport.
  • Breaker — Tries invalid inputs, retries, back navigation, and double submissions.

What does the skill actually do?

It guides your coding agent through a simple process:

  1. Identify what first success means for your app.
  2. Explore the onboarding journey through four different behaviors.
  3. Record blockers with browser evidence and reproduction steps.
  4. Prioritize issues and propose safe technical fixes.
  5. Verify changes through fresh sessions when supported.

The idea is to catch friction that can be easy to overlook when you're already familiar with your product.

Try it with your coding agent

You can install it using the skills CLI, or simply copy this prompt into Claude Code, Codex, or another compatible coding agent:

Install the first-user-audit Agent Skill from:
https://github.com/BarganConstantin/agent-skills

Use the skills CLI:
npx skills add BarganConstantin/agent-skills --skill first-user-audit

Verify that the skill is installed.

Inspect my application and identify the first useful
outcome a new user should reach.

If a safe local or isolated preview environment and
browser automation are available, run the four
first-user personas with fresh browser sessions.

Collect evidence, identify friction, propose bounded
technical fixes, and verify changes with fresh
agent contexts when supported.

Do not use production data or live payments.
Ask before sensitive changes or reduced-isolation runs.

If anything is missing, explain how to set it up.
Never invent test results.

The skill requires connected browser tooling for the audit. Independent subagents depend on your coding environment, and simulated personas don't replace real usability testing.

It's open source under the MIT license.

Did it catch an issue you hadn't noticed? Did it miss something obvious? Was the setup straightforward?
