articles.body_html:
Why Your React Animations Feel Slow Even at 60 FPS

You open the Performance panel. The animation is running around 60 FPS. There are no spectacular red warnings, nothing is visibly freezing, and your laptop is barely interested.

Yet the interaction still feels slow.

The cursor seems to chase the pointer instead of following it. A scroll reveal arrives just after you expect it. A draggable card has a slightly rubbery disconnect from your hand. A menu technically animates smoothly, but opening it feels heavier than clicking the same control without motion.

This is where an FPS counter can send debugging in the wrong direction.

60 FPS tells you how many frames arrived. It does not tell you whether they arrived well.

Animation quality is a combination of frame consistency, input latency, browser rendering work, JavaScript execution and the actual motion decisions you made. React can participate in those problems, but “React is slow” is rarely a useful diagnosis.

The better question is: what kind of slow are you looking at?

60 FPS Is a Target, Not a Diagnosis

On a 60 Hz display, the browser gets a new refresh opportunity roughly every 16.7 milliseconds. During that window it may need to execute JavaScript, recalculate styles, perform layout, paint pixels and composite layers before the updated frame reaches the display.

That is why 60 FPS became a familiar target for interface animation. A consistently delivered frame roughly every 16.7 ms can look smooth on a 60 Hz display.

The important word is consistently.

Imagine an FPS overlay reports an average around 60 over a measurement window. That number does not tell you whether individual frames were evenly spaced. A sequence with occasional slow frames followed by quicker frames can have a respectable average while still producing visible hitching.

Perceived motion follows the spacing of frames, not the optimism of the average.

This is also why hardcoding your animation around an assumption of exactly 60 updates per second is fragile. Displays running at 120 Hz and 144 Hz are common enough that requestAnimationFrame() may be called at those rates instead. MDN explicitly recommends using the timestamp provided to the callback when calculating animation progress.

let start;

function animate(timestamp) {
  if (start === undefined) {
    start = timestamp;
  }

  const elapsed = timestamp - start;
  const progress = Math.min(elapsed / 600, 1);

  element.style.transform = `translateX(${progress * 200}px)`;

  if (progress < 1) {
    requestAnimationFrame(animate);
  }
}

requestAnimationFrame(animate);

The animation above is based on elapsed time rather than “move three pixels every frame.” That distinction keeps the duration stable when the display refresh rate changes.

You can read more about the behavior of requestAnimationFrame() on MDN.

Your Browser Has More Work to Do Than Draw the Animation

When an element changes visually, the browser does not simply receive your new value and teleport pixels into place.

Depending on what changed, it can move through several stages: style recalculation, layout, paint and composition. The amount of work depends partly on the CSS property being animated.

Animating something that changes geometry, such as width, left or margin, can require the browser to recalculate layout and repaint. Properties such as transform and opacity can often avoid layout and be handled later in the rendering pipeline.

Consider a simple horizontal movement.

// Can require layout work as the value changes
<div style={{ left: `${x}px` }} />

// Usually a better fit for visual movement
<div style={{ transform: `translateX(${x}px)` }} />

That does not mean transform is a magic performance keyword. You can animate only transforms and still build a sluggish interaction if each frame also performs expensive JavaScript, reads layout repeatedly, updates a large React subtree, draws an expensive canvas scene or runs several competing effects.

The property is one part of the frame. MDN has a useful breakdown of the browser rendering waterfall and animation property costs.

The practical debugging question is not just “Am I getting 60 FPS?” It is “What work has to complete before each visible update?”

React Can Make the Animation Compete With Your Application

React state is a great way to express application state. It is not automatically the best place to store every intermediate pixel of an animation. Suppose a pointer-following element writes its coordinates into component state for every pointermove event:

import { useState } from "react";

export default function Follower() {
  const [position, setPosition] = useState({ x: 0, y: 0 });

  return (
    <div
      onPointerMove={(event) => {
        setPosition({
          x: event.clientX,
          y: event.clientY,
        });
      }}
    >
      <div
        className="follower"
        style={{
          transform: `translate3d(${position.x}px, ${position.y}px, 0)`,
        }}
      />
    </div>
  );
}

There is nothing inherently invalid about this code. The relevant question is what happens around it.

Every state update schedules React work. If Follower is isolated and the surrounding tree is cheap, the result may be perfectly acceptable. If the update causes substantial component work while other JavaScript is also running, you have made your animation share main-thread time with work that may not need to happen every frame.

For transient per-frame values, a ref or an animation system can sometimes keep React responsible for the meaningful state transition while letting interpolation happen outside repeated component renders.

import { useEffect, useRef } from "react";

export default function Follower() {
  const followerRef = useRef(null);
  const target = useRef({ x: 0, y: 0 });
  const current = useRef({ x: 0, y: 0 });

  useEffect(() => {
    let frameId;

    const tick = () => {
      current.current.x +=
        (target.current.x - current.current.x) * 0.18;

      current.current.y +=
        (target.current.y - current.current.y) * 0.18;

      if (followerRef.current) {
        followerRef.current.style.transform =
          `translate3d(${current.current.x}px, ${current.current.y}px, 0)`;
      }

      frameId = requestAnimationFrame(tick);
    };

    frameId = requestAnimationFrame(tick);

    return () => cancelAnimationFrame(frameId);
  }, []);

  return (
    <div
      onPointerMove={(event) => {
        target.current.x = event.clientX;
        target.current.y = event.clientY;
      }}
    >
      <div ref={followerRef} className="follower" />
    </div>
  );
}

This is not a rule that says “never animate through React state.” It is a separation-of-responsibilities question.

If a value exists mainly to produce another visual frame a few milliseconds later, ask whether the entire React render path needs to know about every intermediate value.

Profile before rewriting it.

requestAnimationFrame() Does Not Make Expensive Work Cheap

Moving code into requestAnimationFrame() is another optimization that can feel more powerful than it is.

requestAnimationFrame() tells the browser you want to run a callback before an upcoming repaint. It gives your animation work a browser-aware scheduling mechanism. It does not reduce the amount of work inside the callback.

This can still be expensive:

function tick() {
  const cards = document.querySelectorAll(".card");

  cards.forEach((card) => {
    const rect = card.getBoundingClientRect();

    card.style.transform =
      `translateY(${window.innerHeight - rect.top}px)`;
  });

  requestAnimationFrame(tick);
}

requestAnimationFrame(tick);

Now you are querying elements, measuring layout and writing styles repeatedly. Put enough work in there and rAF will faithfully schedule an expensive callback every time the browser gives you the chance.

The useful question is:

What am I asking the browser to do inside each frame?

Cache what can be cached. Avoid unnecessary layout measurement inside hot loops. Keep cleanup explicit. Stop loops that no longer have a reason to run.

requestAnimationFrame() is a scheduler, not absolution.

Sometimes the Performance Problem Is Actually a Motion Problem

This is the category that profiling tools cannot solve for you. An interaction can be computationally cheap, maintain a steady frame rate and still feel slow because you told it to move slowly.

Imagine a cursor follower using this interpolation:

current += (target - current) * 0.05;

The browser may render it beautifully. No dropped frames. No expensive layout. No large React commits. It can still feel like the cursor is dragging a reluctant ghost behind it.

Change the interpolation:

current += (target - current) * 0.22;

The computational cost is effectively the same, but the interaction feels radically more immediate.

The same problem appears with animation durations, easing curves and springs. A navigation overlay with a long ease-in can feel resistant because the first part of the motion barely moves. A spring with too little stiffness or too much settling can make a button feel mushy. A parallax layer that deliberately trails scroll position may cross the line from depth into input lag.

A perfectly rendered delay is still a delay.

This matters because developers often respond to that feeling by optimizing code that is already fast enough. They memoize components, switch libraries or reach for will-change, only to discover that the animation still feels heavy.

Before doing that, temporarily shorten the duration or remove smoothing. If the interaction suddenly feels right while the performance trace barely changes, you found a motion-design problem rather than a rendering bottleneck.

Input-Coupled Motion Exposes Latency Faster

Not all animation has the same relationship with the user.

A decorative background can arrive slightly late without anyone having a precise expectation for where it should be. A button pressed under a cursor is different. So is dragging, scrolling, scrubbing or moving a custom pointer.

The user's hand provides a reference signal.

If their pointer is here and your visual follower is consistently there, the delay is obvious. If their finger moves a card and the card takes time to catch up, they feel the gap before they think about it technically.

This is why scroll smoothing deserves restraint. Smoothing the visual response can create a deliberate sense of weight, but too much of it makes the page feel as though scrolling has been routed through syrup.

The same applies to cursor trails. A trailing layer can be expressive while the actual clickable interaction remains immediate. Trouble starts when decorative latency leaks into controls that are supposed to feel direct. For input-driven effects, profile responsiveness and inspect your interpolation before chasing raw FPS.

“Use Transform and Opacity” Is Good Advice With Missing Footnotes

For many DOM animations, transform and opacity are sensible first choices because they can avoid the layout work triggered by geometry-changing properties. They should not become a superstition.

A fullscreen blur, huge translucent layer, complex SVG filter, large shadow or high-resolution canvas may still cost real rendering time even if its position changes through transform. A page running five independently smooth animation loops can become expensive when they all operate together.

Production pages are ecosystems. Your effect does not get a private browser.

This becomes especially noticeable on marketing sites where animation lives beside analytics, hydration, images, video, sliders, third-party scripts and application code. An isolated CodePen can tell you whether the effect works. It cannot tell you what happens after the effect moves into the page that has to ship.

Profile Frame Time, Not Just the Counter

When an animation feels wrong, resist the urge to start changing code randomly.

Reproduce the issue in the environment where it actually matters. Use a production build when possible. Development tooling and extra checks can distort performance characteristics.

Then record the interaction in your browser's Performance panel.

Look at what is occupying the main thread around the problematic frames. Is there a large JavaScript task? Repeated style recalculation? Layout work? Expensive paint? A React render arriving at exactly the wrong moment? Multiple callbacks continuing after their sections have left the viewport?

You are trying to identify a category of failure before choosing a fix.

A useful diagnostic table looks like this:

What you feel Inspect first
Animation visibly jumps Frame timing, long JavaScript tasks, layout and paint
Motion is smooth but follows input late Smoothing, interpolation, input handling and main-thread work
Animation struggles while UI data changes React renders and competing JavaScript
Works on desktop, struggles on phone CPU/GPU cost, image/canvas work and concurrent effects
Smooth everywhere but still feels heavy Duration, easing, distance and spring tuning

For deeper diagnostics, browsers are also gaining visibility into Long Animation Frames, which can help identify work contributing to long frames. Treat it as an additional signal rather than the one universal profiling API; support and tooling still deserve checking for your target browsers.

Test the Page, Not the Demo

An animation should be judged in the page where it will live.

That means testing it beside the real navigation, typography, images, scripts and adjacent interactions. It also means testing the actual devices you care about rather than using a high-end development machine as your minimum specification.

Mobile changes more than available processing power. Pointer assumptions disappear. Viewports become shorter. Touch scrolling behaves differently. Effects that feel appropriately restrained with a mouse can become annoying when attached to every finger movement.

Offscreen work matters too. If a canvas render loop or animation keeps producing frames after the user has left the section, it is still spending resources even though it contributes nothing to the current experience.

The production checklist is therefore broader than “does it hit 60?”

Ask whether the effect stops when appropriate. Ask whether it still reads correctly without motion. Check prefers-reduced-motion where the interaction calls for an alternative. Verify keyboard and touch behavior where controls are involved.

And test the whole page.

Source Access Is Useful Because Performance Decisions Are Contextual

This is also where reusable animation patterns get interesting.

A polished demo can give you the right interaction idea, but production usually requires changing something: timing, breakpoint behavior, scroll distance, pointer behavior, dependencies, cleanup, the number of animated elements, or what happens when motion is reduced.

That is why Hyperiux Vault uses a source-first model for its React and Next.js interaction effects. The effect files land in your project, so the implementation can be inspected and tuned rather than treated as a sealed animation runtime. That does not make an effect automatically fast. It makes the decisions visible.

A scroll interaction may need different behavior on a short mobile viewport. A cursor system should not assume a fine pointer exists on every device. A WebGL scene has a very different rendering budget from a CSS text reveal. Those decisions belong in the implementation, not in a blanket promise that every animation is “optimized.”

Vault's Scroll Effects guidance makes the same production distinction: use properties appropriate for animation, avoid unnecessary layout reads during scroll, clean up timelines and listeners, and test the effect on a real mid-range device before treating the implementation as finished.

If you want a starting point rather than another empty component file, you can browse the React and Next.js interaction effects in Vault and adapt the source to the page that actually has to ship.

A Better Way to Debug “Slow” Animation

The next time an animation looks smooth in an FPS overlay but feels wrong under your hand, split the problem into separate questions.

Is the browser delivering frames consistently? Is expensive work happening during those frames? Is React doing work that does not need to happen at animation frequency? Is the visual response arriving late after input? Or is the easing itself simply telling the interface to feel slow?

Those failures can look similar from the outside, but they need different fixes.

60 FPS is useful evidence. It just isn't a verdict.

articles.title: Locking files in the browser with Web Crypto: PBKDF2, HKDF, and 1 MiB AES-GCM records
articles.description: I built a small web app called Clipboard Share. Devices on the same Wi-Fi network see each other...
articles.body_html:
I built a small web app called Clipboard Share. Devices on the same Wi-Fi network see each other automatically, no sign-up, and you drag a file or paste some text to send it. It was made with Claude Code, and I'm the only person working on it.

The thing about "same network, no account" is that anyone on that network can join the room. That's fine for a meme or a photo. It's less fine for a scan of an ID card or a contract that you want to move to a shared PC.

So I added an opt-in "lock with a password" switch. This post is about how it works, with the real code, and a list of what it still doesn't do. Locking is off by default, and you turn it on per upload.

What I wanted

  • Locking is something you switch on. The normal flow gets no extra clicks.
  • The password and the encryption keys are never sent to the server.
  • Big files still have to work. The design doc says up to 5 GB, so I couldn't encrypt a whole file in memory.

The last point shaped everything else. It led to chunked encryption, a service worker on the download side, and a few details I would have skipped otherwise.

The overall shape

Password → PBKDF2 → HKDF splits it into encKey and verifier → a random per-file key is wrapped with encKey and stored in metadata → the file body is encrypted in 1 MiB AES-GCM records → on download, a service worker decrypts while the bytes arrive.

The server stores ciphertext, the hash of the verifier, the wrapped file key, and the encrypted file name. It never receives the password or encKey.

Step 1: one password, two keys

The password goes through PBKDF2-SHA256 with 600,000 iterations (PBKDF2_ITERATIONS = 600000). The salt is 16 random bytes, generated once each time you set up a lock. Within one session I reuse the derived keys, because running 600,000 iterations per file would be painfully slow.

There's a design problem here. The server has to check that the password is right, so the client has to send something. That something must not be the encryption key. So I split the PBKDF2 output with HKDF into two independent values, using different info strings:

const hkdf = await subtle().importKey('raw', masterBytes, 'HKDF', false, ['deriveBits', 'deriveKey'])
const empty = new Uint8Array(0)
const encKey = await subtle().deriveKey(
  { name: 'HKDF', hash: 'SHA-256', salt: empty, info: INFO_ENC },
  hkdf,
  { name: 'AES-GCM', length: 256 },
  false,
  ['encrypt', 'decrypt']
)
const verifierBits = await subtle().deriveBits({ name: 'HKDF', hash: 'SHA-256', salt: empty, info: INFO_VERIFY }, hkdf, 256)
const vh = toHex(await subtle().digest('SHA-256', verifierBits))

That's deriveLockFromMaster in utils/lockCrypto.js. The info strings are cs-lock-v1/enc and cs-lock-v1/verify. encKey is created with extractable: false, so page JavaScript can use it but can't read the raw bytes.

The server stores only vh, the SHA-256 of the verifier. To unlock, the client sends the verifier and the server hashes it and compares. So the server can recognize the right password, but it can't compute encKey from what it holds.

Step 2: a random key per file

I don't encrypt file contents with encKey directly. Each file gets its own random 32-byte key (the DK). The DK encrypts the body and the file name. encKey only wraps the DK.

wrapFileKey encrypts the DK with AES-GCM under a random 12-byte IV and the additional data cs-lock-v1/key. The result is 48 bytes (32 + the 16-byte tag), which goes into the object metadata along with the IV.

Two things come out of this. Files locked with the same password still have different keys. And the QR link later on can carry the key for one file only, instead of anything password-wide.

The file name is encrypted with the DK too, trimmed to 180 UTF-8 bytes without cutting a character in half and keeping the extension. In the UI, a locked file's card shows random characters instead of its name until it's unlocked.

The uploading device also creates a random 32-byte delete key. Only its SHA-256 (dh) goes to the server. The key itself stays in that device's memory.

Step 3: 1 MiB records

AES-GCM only gives you the plaintext after it has verified the whole message. If I encrypted a 2 GB file as one message, the browser would have to hold all of it, and the receiver couldn't release a single byte until the end.

So the plaintext is cut into 1 MiB records (RECORD_SIZE = 1024 * 1024), and each record is its own AES-GCM message with a 16-byte tag. The IV is a random 4-byte per-file prefix plus the record index as a 64-bit big-endian number. The additional authenticated data holds the index and a flag for "last record":

export function recordAad(index, isLast) {
  const aad = new Uint8Array(AAD_RECORD_PREFIX.length + 9)
  aad.set(AAD_RECORD_PREFIX, 0)
  const view = new DataView(aad.buffer)
  writeU64(view, AAD_RECORD_PREFIX.length, index)
  aad[aad.length - 1] = isLast ? 1 : 0
  return aad
}

The last-record flag matters. With independently authenticated records, chopping the end off a file leaves every earlier record valid, so a truncated file would decrypt "successfully" into a shorter one. With the flag in the AAD, the new final record fails authentication because it wasn't encrypted as the last one. The decryptor's finish() also checks that exactly the expected number of records arrived (LOCK_TRUNCATED, LOCK_TRAILING_DATA).

Uploading reuses the existing multipart uploader. The server is told it's receiving a "virtual file" the size of the ciphertext. One part is 64 records, which is 64 × (1 MiB + 16) bytes of ciphertext. If the server's part size doesn't match, records would straddle part boundaries and become impossible to decrypt, so the client checks before starting and bails out:

const created = await baseApi.create(rid, { size: pt, lock: meta })
if (created.partSize !== CT_PART_SIZE) {
  // 파트 경계가 다르면 레코드가 파트 사이에 걸쳐 풀 수 없게 된다 → 시작하지 않는다
  try { await baseApi.abort(rid, { uploadId: created.uploadId, key: created.key, size: total }) } catch { /* ignore */ }
  throw Object.assign(new Error('Unexpected part size'), { code: 'LOCK_PART_SIZE', retryable: false })
}

(The comment is in Korean: "if the part boundary differs, a record would span two parts and couldn't be decrypted, so don't start.")

Each part is encrypted just before it's uploaded, reading only that slice of the file (encryptPart), so the full file never sits in memory. One limitation: locked uploads don't save resume state to localStorage. Retries during a session work, but you can't close the tab and resume later.

Step 4: decrypting while downloading

Downloading a multi-gigabyte ciphertext and decrypting afterwards would crash a phone. Instead, a service worker intercepts requests to /__locked/<token>, decrypts records as the bytes arrive, and streams the plaintext to the browser, which treats it as a normal download.

const body = new ReadableStream({
  async pull(controller) {
    for (;;) {
      const { done, value } = await reader.read()
      if (done) {
        decryptor.finish()
        controller.close()
        return
      }
      const out = await decryptor.push(value)
      if (out.length > 0) {
        for (const pt of out) controller.enqueue(pt)
        return
      }
    }
  }
})

That's trimmed from handleLockedDownload in public/sw.js; I removed progress notifications and error handling. The decryptor accepts chunks of any size, buffers them, and returns plaintext whenever a full record is available.

Service workers aren't bundled in this project, so sw.js can't import lockCrypto.js. The decryption logic exists twice. It's ugly, but a test checks the worker's copy too.

The key goes to the worker through a MessageChannel as a one-time job with a random token. Jobs expire after two minutes (LOCKED_JOB_TTL_MS) and are deleted the first time they're used.

When there's no active service worker controller, or the device is iOS, the app falls back to in-memory decryption. That path refuses files over 500 MB (MEMORY_DECRYPT_LIMIT) and tells the user to download from another device. I haven't tested large files on real devices well enough to quote a real-world ceiling, so I'm not going to.

Step 5: attempt limits per password, not per file

A password is only as strong as the effort needed to guess it, so wrong guesses are rate limited on the server. My first thought was per file, but then N files locked with the same password would give an attacker N times the attempts. So the counter is keyed by vh, one bucket for everything locked with that password:

export const UNLOCK_MAX_TOTAL = 30;
export const UNLOCK_MAX_PER_IP = 5;

export function unlockRemaining(vh: string, ipKey: string, now: number = Date.now()): number {
    const e = entries.get(vh);
    if (!e || now - e.at > ENTRY_TTL_MS) return Math.min(UNLOCK_MAX_TOTAL, UNLOCK_MAX_PER_IP);
    const ip = e.perIp.get(ipKey) ?? 0;
    return Math.max(0, Math.min(UNLOCK_MAX_TOTAL - e.total, UNLOCK_MAX_PER_IP - ip));
}

There are 30 wrong guesses total and 5 per IP, whichever runs out first.

The delete endpoint shares the same counter. If deleting accepted a verifier without limits, it would be an unlimited password-guessing oracle, which would make the limit pointless.

Deleting requires proof of one of two things: the delete key from the uploading device (hashed and compared with the stored dh), or the password verifier. Neither means a 403. Comparisons use timingSafeEqual. The unlock endpoint only hands out a presigned download URL after the verifier matches, and that URL lives for 60 seconds (LOCKED_DOWNLOAD_EXPIRES_SEC). Locked objects also sit in a separate R2 bucket (R2_LOCKED_BUCKET_NAME).

Step 6: QR links with the key after the #

Typing a password on a phone is annoying, so every locked file has a "share by QR code" action. The link looks like this:

{origin}/#/lk?r={roomId}&i={id}&v={verifier}&k={file key}

Everything is after the #, so it isn't sent in HTTP requests to the server or CDN. k is the DK of that one file. The password and encKey are not in the link. v is the verifier the server needs before it gives out a download URL.

export function buildLockedLink(origin, { roomId, id, verifier, key }) {
  const q = new URLSearchParams({ r: roomId, i: id, v: verifier, k: key })
  return `${origin}/${LOCKED_LINK_PREFIX}${q.toString()}`
}

index.html strips the fragment from the address bar before the analytics script runs and keeps it only in window.__csLockedLink. When the link is opened, the app uses k to decrypt the file name; if that fails, it reports LOCK_LINK_INVALID.

Anyone who has the link or a photo of the QR code can download that file without the password. You can only create one if you locked the file yourself or confirmed the password in this session.

What's still not good

I'd rather list the limits than have somebody find them.

1. The password lock doesn't cover text or device info. It protects files and file names. Text you send, the animal-name labels for devices, file sizes and upload times are all visible. Text locking was pushed to a second phase in the design doc.

2. Browser crypto means trusting the JavaScript the server sends. The encryption runs in your browser, but the site delivers the code. If the site's code were changed, the browser-side encryption wouldn't help. Every web app that does crypto in the page has this limit. The accurate summary for files you lock with a password is: if you received the genuine code, the password isn't sent to the server. It's not "the server can never see anything."

3. The verifier is per password, not per file. The v in a QR link comes from the password. So with the same password on several files in one room, someone holding one QR link can also ask the server to download or delete the other files' ciphertext. They still can't decrypt those files, because k is per file, but the delete request is a real gap.

4. Attempt counters live in server memory. It's a Map. Restart the server and the counters reset. The design doc lists this as a known limit, and I haven't moved it to persistent storage. Related: the same doc notes that whoever holds the server's vh and a ciphertext could try short passwords offline. PBKDF2 at 600,000 iterations slows that down but doesn't remove it. The input currently only requires 4 characters (MIN_LOCK_PASSWORD = 4).

And there's no recovery. If you forget the password, the file stays locked. Locked files are kept like regular ones: they're deleted soon after everyone leaves, and at most about a day.

Wrap-up

PBKDF2 at 600,000 iterations, HKDF to separate encKey and verifier, a wrapped random key per file, 1 MiB AES-GCM records with a last-record flag, a service worker that decrypts as bytes arrive, and attempt limits counted per password. If you spot something wrong, especially in the crypto, please tell me.

You can try it here:

https://www.clipboardapp.org

Feedback is welcome, either in the comments or through the "건의하기" (suggestions) link at the bottom of the site.

Originally published in Korean on velog.

articles.title: I built a 3D free-kick game in three.js: Magnus curl in 10 lines, floodlights and a keeper that reads your shot
articles.description: I'm a solo dev and I just shipped Efectazo, a free free-kick football game that runs in the browser,...
articles.body_html:
I'm a solo dev and I just shipped Efectazo, a free free-kick football game that runs in the browser, on phones and desktop: https://efectazo.pages.dev

You swipe to shoot, and the shape of your swipe becomes curl on the ball. Here's how the main pieces work.

The ball: gravity, drag and a Magnus force

The physics module is plain JS with no three.js in it, so I can run it headless in tests. Each substep adds three forces to the ball:

// Magnus: CM * (w x v)
export function accel(b, wind) {
  const [vx, vy, vz] = b.v;
  const rx = vx - wind[0], rz = vz - wind[1];
  const sp = Math.hypot(rx, vy, rz);
  const [wx, wy, wz] = b.w;
  const mx = wy * rz - wz * vy, my = wz * rx - wx * rz, mz = wx * vy - wy * rx;
  return [-KD * sp * rx + CM * mx,
          -G - KD * sp * vy + CM * my,
          -KD * sp * rz + CM * mz];
}

Quadratic drag slows the ball, and the cross product of spin and velocity pushes it sideways (side spin) or down (topspin dip). Spin decays exponentially, so the bend gets stronger late in the flight, which is what makes a good free kick look right.

From swipe to shot

  • Direction comes from the first 40% of the swipe
  • Power from swipe speed, height from swipe length
  • Side spin from how much the swipe curves

So if you draw a banana, the ball bends like one.

The goalkeeper

The keeper has a reaction delay, predicts where the ball will cross the line (better keepers read the curl better), and dives with limited speed and reach. A save only happens when the ball actually hits his limbs, so it never feels scripted. The wall (0 to 6 players) jumps when you kick.

Rendering

  • three.js r160, MeshStandard/Physical materials, PMREM image-based lighting
  • Two shadow-casting "floodlight" directional lights with PCF soft shadows
  • A procedural grass shader (mowing stripes plus detail noise) instead of a big texture
  • ACES filmic tone mapping, bloom, and a slow-motion replay with depth of field after goals
  • Quality tiers with an Auto mode that drops a tier if the frame rate stays under ~47 fps for 2 seconds, which matters a lot on phones

The game around it

40 career levels, a seeded Daily Challenge (5 shots, with an emoji grid you can share), an endless Arcade mode and Cups. Coins unlock balls, boots, kits, stadiums (night, day, sunset, rain, snow) and celebrations. English and Spanish. It's free, with an optional one-time Pro upgrade.

Play it here: https://efectazo.pages.dev (also on itch: https://nightlit.itch.io/efectazo)

I'd love to hear how it runs on your device and how the curl feels. Happy to go deeper on any part in the comments.

articles.title: How I Convert PDF to Markdown in the Browser
articles.description: I built a browser-based PDF to Markdown converter. I expected parsing the PDF to be the hard part. It...
articles.body_html:
I built a browser-based PDF to Markdown converter. I expected parsing the PDF to be the hard part. It wasn't: PDF.js handles that.

The hard part is that a PDF has no paragraphs, headings or lists. Word stores "this is Heading 2". HTML stores <h2>. A PDF stores "draw these glyphs at 16pt at (89.8, 751.4)". It's a list of drawing instructions for a printer.

So PDF to Markdown is reverse engineering: look at where text is drawn and how big it is, and guess the structure the author had in mind. This post walks through the rules I ended up with, with the real code, and the bugs that forced each one.

What PDF.js gives you

page.getTextContent() returns text items. Here's a simplified excerpt from page 1 of a real 4-page PDF:

{ "str": "Academic & Creative", "transform": [14, 0, 0, 14, 89.8, 188.6] }
{ "str": "", "transform": [16, 0, 0, 16, 89.8, 751.4], "hasEOL": true }
{ "str": "MD-to.com PDF Converter — Feature Guide", "transform": [16, 0, 0, 16, 89.8, 751.4] }
{ "str": "Download PDF", "transform": [11, 0, 0, 11, 376.7, 689.2] }
{ "str": "Try it now: paste any Markdown on the left and click", "transform": [11, 0, 0, 11, 89.8, 689.2] }

transform is a 2D matrix: the last two values are x and y, and the font size is in the first four. Things to notice:

  1. Item order isn't reading order. The first item is near the bottom of the page. "Download PDF" comes before "Try it now", but it's to its right on the same line.
  2. y points up. The origin is the bottom-left corner.
  3. Empty items carry nothing but a hasEOL flag.
  4. Font names are useless. fontName is an internal ID like g_d0_f1, so at this level you can't tell whether text is bold.

The pipeline 

PDF.js (parsing)
  └─ pdfjs-adapter: normalize coordinates → { str, x, y, width, height }
      └─ pdf-reader: per page, progress, cancel, isolate failed pages
          └─ pdf-extraction (pure functions):
               items → lines → drop headers/footers → body font size
               → headings / paragraphs / lists → escape → Markdown

The key design decision: the structure inference doesn't know about PDF.js. It takes plain { str, x, y, width, height } objects and returns a string. That made it testable with hand-written coordinates, which turned out to be the most valuable thing in the whole project.

The adapter flips the y axis to screen space (y grows downward) and takes the font size from the matrix, so scaled text gets its real size:

const viewport = page.getViewport({ scale: 1 });
const transform = pdfjs.Util.transform(viewport.transform, item.transform);
return {
  str: item.str,
  x: transform[4],
  y: transform[5],
  width: item.width,
  height: Math.hypot(transform[2], transform[3]) || item.height,
};

Step 1: Items → lines

Drop empty items, sort by y then x, and put items on the same line when their y values are close:

Math.abs(last.y - item.y) <= Math.max(2, Math.min(last.height, item.height) * 0.3)

30% of the font size absorbs superscripts, baseline differences between fonts and floating-point noise, without merging two real lines.

When do you insert a space?

Generators split text however they like: per word, per glyph, or mid-word because of kerning or a font change. Joining with '' glues English words together. Joining with ' ' breaks words in half. So the joiner looks at the actual gap:

// Scripts written without spaces between words. Korean (Hangul) separates
// words with spaces, so it follows the same gap rules as Latin text.
const cjk = /[\p{Script=Han}\p{Script=Hiragana}\p{Script=Katakana}]/u;

function separator(left: string, right: string, gap?: number, height = 12) {
  if (!left || !right || /\s$/.test(left) || /^\s/.test(right)) return '';
  // Gap under 12% of the font size: one word split into two runs
  if (gap !== undefined && gap <= Math.max(0.5, height * 0.12)) return '';
  // No space before punctuation or after an opening bracket
  if (/^[，。！？、；：）》」』】〕,.!?;:)]/u.test(right) || /[（《「『【〔(]$/u.test(left))
    return '';
  if (cjk.test(left.at(-1)!) && cjk.test(right[0])) return '';
  return ' ';
}

Hel + lo with gap 0 → Hello. Hello + world with gap 6 → Hello world. Two Chinese runs → no space.

That comment about Korean is there because of a bug. The first version used "CJK" to mean Chinese, Japanese and Korean. But Korean separates words with spaces. I only caught it while testing a Korean PDF: 보고서를 + 작성합니다. came out as 보고서를작성합니다.

Even after the fix, one case can't be solved. Korean text can wrap between words or between syllables, and I generated both kinds of PDF in Chrome to compare. In both, the line ends with no trailing space and nothing in the data says "this break was mid-word". I chose to add a space across line breaks, because wrapping between words is more common. PDFs that wrap mid-word get an extra space at the break.

Step 2: Headers and footers

My first version deleted any line that was 1–4 digits or looked like Page 3 of 10. It deleted the year 2026 from body text and numbers from tables, and missed the actual running header, which wasn't a number.

Now each line gets a "margin key", and a key is only removed if it repeats across pages:

function marginKey(line: Line, page: PdfPageText): string | undefined {
  const relative = line.y / page.height;
  // Only the top or bottom 5% of the page, and only short lines
  if (!(relative < 0.05 || relative > 0.95) || line.text.length > 80) return;
  const edge = relative < 0.05 ? 'top' : 'bottom';
  const number =
    line.text.match(/^(?:page\s+)?(\d+)(?:\s+of\s+\d+)?$/i) ||
    line.text.match(/^-\s*(\d+)\s*-$/);
  if (number) {
    // Ambiguous numbers, years and amounts survive, even near a page edge.
    return Number(number[1]) === page.number ? `${edge}:page-number` : undefined;
  }
  return `${edge}:${Math.round(relative * 100)}:${line.text}`;
}

A key is removed only if it appears on at least max(2, ceil(pages × 0.6)) pages. Page numbers 3 on page 3 and 4 on page 4 share the key bottom:page-number, so they're removed together. A 2026 near the edge doesn't match the page number, so it stays.

This is deliberately conservative. Roman numerals and numbering that starts after the cover aren't removed. A leftover page number is obvious. A deleted sentence may never be noticed. The UI also tells the user how many header and footer lines were removed.

Step 3: Headings from font size

First, find the body font size, weighting each size by character count rather than line count, across the whole document:

function bodyFontSize(lines: Line[]) {
  const weights = new Map<number, number>();
  for (const line of lines) {
    const size = Math.round(line.height);
    weights.set(size, (weights.get(size) || 0) + line.text.length);
  }
  return [...weights].sort((a, b) => b[1] - a[1])[0]?.[0] || 12;
}

Counting lines would let short headings and page numbers outvote long paragraphs. In the 4-page sample, 11pt had 2,146 characters, 10pt (code) 350, 16pt 184 and 14pt 119, so body text is 11pt.

Each line's size divided by the body size gives the heading level:

Ratio to body size Output
≥ 2 #
≥ 1.6 ##
> 1.3 ###
≤ 1.3 paragraph

In the sample, 16pt headings (ratio 1.45) became ###. The 14pt sub-headings (1.27) stayed as paragraphs. A lower threshold would catch them, but in another document with 10pt body and 12pt quotes, every quote would become a heading. No threshold fits every PDF, so this one leans careful, and the UI has a switch to turn heading detection off.

The feature that never worked

The first version also had bold detection: same size as body, short, bold → **sub-heading**. It checked whether the font name contained bold, heavy or black.

During the rewrite I realized this had never fired. Font names are g_d0_f1. I deleted it. A feature that looks like it works but doesn't is worse than no feature. Reading real font names from PDF.js font objects is on the list for later.

Step 4: Paragraphs and lists

Two signals start a new paragraph:

const verticalBreak = gap > Math.max(line.height, previous?.height || 0) * 1.8;
// Only a rightward shift is a first-line indent; returning to the left
// margin is the rest of that paragraph.
const paragraph = verticalBreak || (previous && line.x - previous.x > line.height);

Line spacing in body text is usually 1.2–1.5× the line height, and there's extra space between paragraphs, so 1.8× sits in between. Many documents, especially Chinese ones, use first-line indentation and no spacing at all. Only a shift to the right counts. The line after an indented first line moves left again, and that's the same paragraph. One version split every indented paragraph in two before I added that comment.

Lists start with •, ◦, -, *, 1., 1) and so on. The hard part is wrapped items:

• First item that wraps
  onto a second line        ← hanging indent: same item
• Second item
Independent text            ← back at the margin: not a list item

I got this wrong in both directions. Version one appended any line without a paragraph gap to the previous block, so Independent text was swallowed into the last list item. A later version split onto a second line into its own paragraph and broke the list in two.

The rule now: a line continues a list item if there's no vertical break and it starts to the right of the bullet:

} else if (
  last?.kind === 'list' &&
  !verticalBreak &&
  line.x - last.x! > Math.max(1, line.height * 0.2)
) {
  // Hanging-indent line continues the current list item.

Output:

- First item that wraps onto a second line
- Second item

Independent text

Step 5: Escaping, but not too much

Text in a PDF is literal. # tag at the start of a line is a hashtag, not a heading. The first version escaped nothing, so lines starting with # became headings, <b>literal</b> rendered as bold, and a line like --- | --- turned the line above it into a table header.

Escaping every Markdown character caused a different bug: citations like [1] rendered as math. My renderer supports KaTeX, and \[ ... \] is the display math delimiter. A standard escaper turns [1] into \[1\], which most renderers show as [1]. Mine showed an equation.

So the escaper only touches characters in positions where they would trigger syntax:

export function escapePdfText(text: string) {
  const escaped = text
    .replace(/[\\`*$]/g, '\\$&')
    // Only underscores that could start emphasis; snake_case stays as is
    .replace(/(?<![\p{L}\p{N}])_|_(?![\p{L}\p{N}])/gu, '\\_')
    .replace(/~(?=~)|(?<=~)~/g, '\\~')
    // `]` only before ( [ : — links, images, references. `[` is never escaped.
    .replace(/\](?=[([:])/g, '\\]')
    .replace(/\^(?=\[)/g, '\\^')
    .replace(/<(?=[\p{L}/!?])/gu, '\\<')
    .replace(/&(?=#\d+;|#x[\da-f]+;|[a-z][\da-z]*;)/gi, '\\&')
    // Line-start blocks: headings, quotes, lists, setext underlines and rules
    .replace(/^(?:#|>|[-+](?=\s|$)|[-=](?=[-=\s]*$))/, '\\$&')
    .replace(/^(\d+)([.)])(?=\s|$)/, '$1\\$2');
  // A delimiter row such as `--- | ---` would turn the previous line into a table
  return /^[\s|:\\-]*\|[\s|:\\-]*$/.test(escaped) && escaped.includes('-')
    ? escaped.replace(/\|/g, '\\|')
    : escaped;
}

snake_case, C#, AT&T, 5 > 3 and [1] pass through unchanged. A line starting with 1. becomes 1\. so it doesn't turn into a list.

The test for this renders escaped strings with the site's own Markdown renderer and checks that the output text matches the input. Testing against a generic renderer wouldn't have caught [1], because that bug only exists with KaTeX enabled.

Step 6: Never compare coordinates across pages

The first version concatenated lines from all pages and then grouped paragraphs. But every page's coordinates start from zero. If the last line of page 1 was at y = 680 and the first line of page 2 was also at 680, the gap was 0, and the two pages became one paragraph.

Now every page is rendered on its own and joined with a blank line:

// Never compare Y coordinates or merge paragraphs across page boundaries.
markdown: filtered
  .map((page) => renderPage(page, bodySize, options))
  .filter(Boolean)
  .join('\n\n'),

The trade-off: a paragraph that continues on the next page gets split. Deleting one blank line fixes that. Two unrelated pages merged into one paragraph is much harder to spot.

Testing a guessing algorithm

Heuristics have one big risk: fixing one case breaks another. Since the inference is pure, every bug above became a test with hand-written coordinates, run with Node's built-in node:test:

const item = (str, y = 100, x = 30, width = str.length * 6) =>
  ({ str, y, x, width, height: 12 });

test('glyph runs infer word gaps without splitting adjacent characters', () => {
  assert.equal(
    extractPdfLines([item('Hello', 100, 30, 30), item('world', 100, 66)])[0].text,
    'Hello world',
  );
  assert.equal(
    extractPdfLines([item('Hel', 100, 30, 18), item('lo', 100, 48)])[0].text,
    'Hello',
  );
});

There are tests for each bug in this post: years surviving the margin filter, Korean spacing, first-line indents, list items swallowing paragraphs, [1] turning into math, --- | --- creating a table, and equal coordinates on different pages.

A second layer builds tiny but valid PDF files in code (a few objects plus an xref table) and runs them through the real PDF.js. That catches the other class of bug, where the pure function is right but PDF.js returns data different from what I assumed.

A few engineering details

  • One bad page doesn't fail the document. A page that throws is marked failed, the rest still convert, and the status bar lists failed pages and pages with no text (scans or blank pages) instead of a generic error.
  • Cancellation. Every async step races against a cancel promise, the PDF.js loading task is destroyed exactly once, and the loop yields with setTimeout(0) after each page so large files don't freeze the tab.
  • The worker is bundled, not loaded from a CDN, so its version always matches the installed PDF.js.

What coordinates can't tell you

  • Tables come out as rows of text. There's no border or column-alignment analysis.
  • Multi-column layouts get interleaved, because items at the same y become one line.
  • Hyphenated line breaks like inter- / national come out as inter- national. There's no reliable way to tell layout hyphens from real ones, so I don't guess.
  • Code indentation, formula structure and images aren't in the text layer in a recoverable form.
  • Scanned PDFs have no text layer and need OCR.

Marker, MinerU and Docling solve these with layout and OCR models, and they do it better. They also need a Python environment or a server upload. This converter goes the other way: rules only, in the browser, no upload, results in seconds for ordinary text PDFs. They're tools for different jobs.

Next on the list, each only once there are enough counter-examples in the tests: real font weights for bold, merging paragraphs across pages when the first page's line has no closing punctuation and the next starts lowercase, column detection from vertical whitespace bands, and simple table recovery from stable x alignment.

The question behind every rule

Almost every bug came from one wrong assumption: reading a PDF as a structured document. It's drawing instructions. So every rule answers one question: if this guess is wrong, what does it cost the user?

  • Headers and footers: keep a page number rather than delete a sentence
  • Headings: miss a heading rather than promote every quote
  • Pages: split a paragraph rather than merge two pages
  • Escaping: escape only what triggers syntax, so [1] stays [1]
  • Bold detection: a broken feature is worse than none

The converter is free at https://md-to.com/pdf-to-markdown and runs entirely in your browser. If you have a text PDF it gets wrong, tell me about it in the comments. Every counter-example becomes a test case.

articles.title: You should use Map instead of object literals for lookup tables
articles.description: A while ago I wrote an article about using object literals instead of switch statements, and I still...
articles.body_html:
A while ago I wrote an article about using object literals instead of switch statements, and I still think the idea behind it is a good one: map an input to an output, skip the long list of case and break, and keep your code short and readable.

But there's a catch I didn't cover back then, and a reader (thanks Dario!) pointed it out in the comments: plain objects don't only contain the keys you put in them.

So in this article I want to show you what the problem is, and why today I'd reach for a Map instead.

A quick recap

In the previous article we had something like this:

const getAnimalSound = animal => {
  const sounds = {
    dog: 'woof',
    cat: 'meow',
    cow: 'moo',
    default: 'unknown sound',
  };

  return sounds[animal] || sounds.default;
};

console.log(getAnimalSound('dog'));   // 'woof'
console.log(getAnimalSound('tiger')); // 'unknown sound'

Clean, short, and it works. Or at least it looks like it does.

So what's the problem?

Every object you create with {} inherits from Object.prototype. This means that when you read sounds[animal], if JavaScript doesn't find the key on the object itself, it goes up the prototype chain and looks there too.

And Object.prototype has quite a few properties on it, like constructor, toString, valueOf, hasOwnProperty and __proto__.

Let's see what happens if we pass one of those names to our function:

console.log(getAnimalSound('constructor')); // [Function: Object]
console.log(getAnimalSound('toString'));    // [Function: toString]
console.log(getAnimalSound('__proto__'));   // [Object: null prototype] {}

None of those return 'unknown sound'. Because the value we get back is truthy, the || sounds.default fallback never kicks in, and we return something completely unexpected.

Now, you might think "who would ever pass constructor as an animal?". And you are probably right, until that value comes from a query string, a form field, or the body of an API request. Then anybody can pass whatever they want.

It gets worse with functions

In the previous article we also used object literals to dispatch commands:

const executeCommand = command => {
  const commands = {
    greet: () => console.log('Hello there!'),
    farewell: () => console.log('Goodbye!'),
    default: () => console.log('Unknown command'),
  };

  (commands[command] || commands.default)();
};

Let's try a few "commands":

executeCommand('constructor');    // nothing happens, it silently calls Object()
executeCommand('toString');       // nothing happens either
executeCommand('hasOwnProperty'); // TypeError: Cannot convert undefined or null to object

The first two fail silently, which is the worst kind of bug, because you don't even know something went wrong. The last one crashes your function.

And with nested objects

The state machine example is my favourite one:

const stateTransitions = {
  idle: { start: 'loading' },
  loading: { success: 'loaded', error: 'error' },
};

const handleStateTransition = (currentState, action) =>
  stateTransitions[currentState]?.[action] || currentState;

console.log(handleStateTransition('constructor', 'name')); // 'Object'
console.log(handleStateTransition('idle', 'toString'));    // [Function: toString]

Yes, your component is now in the 'Object' state, or worse, its state is a function.

Note
To be clear, this is not prototype pollution. Prototype pollution happens when an attacker manages to write to Object.prototype, for example with obj[key] = value where key is __proto__. Here we are only reading, but it's still a real bug, and it's the reason why security linters like eslint-plugin-security flag obj[variable] lookups.

Enter Map

A Map is a built-in collection of key/value pairs, and the important difference is that map.get(key) only returns entries that you explicitly added. There's no prototype chain to walk through, so constructor is just a key like any other, and since you never added it, you get undefined.

Let's rewrite our first example:

const sounds = new Map([
  ['dog', 'woof'],
  ['cat', 'meow'],
  ['cow', 'moo'],
]);

const getAnimalSound = animal => sounds.get(animal) ?? 'unknown sound';

console.log(getAnimalSound('dog'));         // 'woof'
console.log(getAnimalSound('tiger'));       // 'unknown sound'
console.log(getAnimalSound('constructor')); // 'unknown sound' ✅
console.log(getAnimalSound('__proto__'));   // 'unknown sound' ✅

You might have noticed a few other small changes, and they are not random:

  • The Map is defined outside the function, so we don't rebuild it every time the function is called.
  • The fallback is no longer stored as a default key, so nobody can "select" it by passing 'default'.
  • I'm using ?? (nullish coalescing) instead of ||. With ||, a valid value like 0 or an empty string would be replaced by the fallback. With ??, the fallback is used only when the value is null or undefined.

Tip
If you already have an object and you don't want to rewrite it as an array of arrays, you can convert it with new Map(Object.entries(myObject)).

Dispatching functions

The same works for our commands:

const commands = new Map([
  ['greet', () => console.log('Hello there!')],
  ['farewell', () => console.log('Goodbye!')],
  ['time', () => console.log(`Current time: ${new Date().toLocaleTimeString()}`)],
]);

const unknownCommand = () => console.log('Unknown command');

const executeCommand = command => (commands.get(command) ?? unknownCommand)();

executeCommand('greet');          // 'Hello there!'
executeCommand('hasOwnProperty'); // 'Unknown command' ✅

And with parameters, like the calculator from the previous article:

const operations = new Map([
  ['add', (x, y) => x + y],
  ['subtract', (x, y) => x - y],
  ['multiply', (x, y) => x * y],
  ['divide', (x, y) => (y !== 0 ? x / y : 'Cannot divide by zero')],
]);

const calculator = (a, b, operation) => {
  const fn = operations.get(operation);
  return fn ? fn(a, b) : 'Unknown operation';
};

console.log(calculator(5, 3, 'add'));     // 8
console.log(calculator(5, 3, 'valueOf')); // 'Unknown operation' ✅

The state machine

For nested lookups you can nest Maps too:

const stateTransitions = new Map([
  ['idle', new Map([['start', 'loading'], ['reset', 'idle']])],
  ['loading', new Map([['success', 'loaded'], ['error', 'error'], ['cancel', 'idle']])],
  ['loaded', new Map([['refresh', 'loading'], ['clear', 'idle']])],
  ['error', new Map([['retry', 'loading'], ['clear', 'idle']])],
]);

const handleStateTransition = (currentState, action) =>
  stateTransitions.get(currentState)?.get(action) ?? currentState;

let state = 'idle';
state = handleStateTransition(state, 'start');    // 'loading'
state = handleStateTransition(state, 'success');  // 'loaded'
state = handleStateTransition(state, 'toString'); // 'loaded' (unchanged) ✅

I'll be honest, this one is a bit less pretty than the object version. We'll come back to that in a moment.

A bonus with TypeScript

If you use TypeScript, Map has another nice side effect: map.get() always returns T | undefined, so the compiler forces you to handle the missing case.

type Animal = 'dog' | 'cat' | 'cow';

const sounds = new Map<Animal, string>([
  ['dog', 'woof'],
  ['cat', 'meow'],
  ['cow', 'moo'],
]);

const getAnimalSound = (animal: Animal): string =>
  sounds.get(animal) ?? 'unknown sound'; // without ?? TypeScript will complain

When you don't need a Map

As always, I don't want you to take this as "never use objects again". There are cases where a plain object is perfectly fine.

When the keys never come from outside your code. If the key is a value you control, for example a TypeScript literal union that you pass around internally, the prototype issue can't really happen. In that case an object with satisfies gives you great type checking:

type Animal = 'dog' | 'cat' | 'cow';

const sounds = {
  dog: 'woof',
  cat: 'meow',
  cow: 'moo',
} satisfies Record<Animal, string>;

Just remember that TypeScript types disappear at runtime: if the value comes from a request or a form, you still need to validate it.

When you only need a quick safety check. If you want to keep the object syntax, Object.hasOwn() checks only the object's own properties, ignoring the prototype chain:

const getAnimalSound = animal =>
  Object.hasOwn(sounds, animal) ? sounds[animal] : 'unknown sound';

This is also a good option for deeply nested tables like the state machine, where nested Maps get a bit noisy.

When you need to serialise the data. JSON.stringify(new Map([['a', 1]])) returns {}, not what you expect. If your lookup table needs to be sent over the wire or saved as JSON, an object is easier to work with.

When switch is simply the better tool. As I mentioned in the previous article, if your conditions involve ranges, complex expressions or intentional fall-through, a switch is still the right choice.

Conclusions

Object literals are still a great idea to replace long switch statements, but when the key comes from user input, a plain object can return things you never put in it, like constructor or toString.

A Map fixes that by design: it only knows the keys you gave it, it works nicely with ??, and with TypeScript it forces you to handle the missing case.

So my rule of thumb today is simple:

  • If the key comes from outside your code, use a Map.
  • If the key is fully under your control, an object is fine, and Object.hasOwn() is a cheap safety net if you want one.

I hope this helped you to understand the hidden gotcha of object lookups, and as always any comments are welcome!

Disclaimer

Parts of this article were created with the help of AI.

articles.title: In an AI security audit, the skeptic is the product
articles.description: I wrote four security findings against a 47-line Node service. Two of them were false. One cites a...
articles.body_html:
I wrote four security findings against a 47-line Node service. Two of them were false. One cites a file that does not exist.

Cloudflare's findings validator passed all four.

That is not a bug in the validator. It is the clearest way I found to show where the value of an AI security review actually sits.

The skill

cloudflare/security-audit-skill is a coding-agent skill that turns one agent into a coordinator of many: recon agents map the code, hunter agents look for bugs, and fresh verifier agents try to knock each finding down before it reaches a report. It was on GitHub trending this week with almost 2,000 stars in a day, 35,690 in total when I checked. MIT licensed. Cloudflare says it is the starting point of the vulnerability harness they now run across their whole fleet.

I measured it before reading it closely. The skill is 15 markdown files: 1,778 lines, 24,768 words, about 183 KB. At the usual four bytes per token that is roughly 46,000 tokens of instructions, loaded in pieces as a run needs them. Cloudflare's blog post says the first version was about 450 lines.

Two zero-dependency Node scripts sit beside the prose: validate-findings.cjs (773 lines) and validate-coverage-ledger.cjs (872 lines). Their own test suites ran clean on my machine, 34 and 31 tests.

The part that caught my eye is the proportion. Of the six phases, two exist only to disprove: Phase 3 hands every candidate to a fresh agent told to refute it, and Phase 5 sends another fresh agent over the final record (the quick profile merges the two). Each Phase 3 verifier prompt carries about 17.5 KB of fixed text before it sees the candidate: a six-step refutation prompt, a file-promotion procedure, and three schema branches copied in verbatim.

What I actually did

I did not install the skill, and no agent ran it. The README's install path is a skills CLI that writes into your agent's config, and I don't do that for a post.

Instead I wrote a small target, played the hunter by hand, and ran the skill's real validator on the result. The target is a notes service on node:http and node:sqlite with dummy users alice and bob. These are the two functions that matter:

function search(user, q) {
  const sql = "SELECT id, title FROM notes WHERE owner = '" + user + "' AND title LIKE '%" + q + "%'";
  return db.prepare(sql).all();
}

function getNote(user, id) {
  return db.prepare('SELECT id, title, body FROM notes WHERE id = ? AND owner = ?').get(id, user);
}

There is also an /admin/export route gated on X-Forwarded-For starting with 10..

Then I wrote four findings the way a hunter returns them, in the skill's schema:

  1. SQL injection in search. Real.
  2. SQL injection in getNote, marked confirmed, with an observed result claiming it returned bob's note. False.
  3. SQL injection in findUser at src/users.js line 212. Invented: that file does not exist.
  4. The export gate trusts a header a client can set, unless a proxy rewrites it. A real question, but the proxy is not in the repo.

What the validator checks 

$ node validate-findings.cjs proposed.json
PASS: 4 findings valid

To be fair to it, it does enforce the contract. When I raised one record's overall severity above its impact, or put a severity on the needs_validation record, it failed, with exact paths. It checks shape, ordering, safe relative paths, and that a confirmed record has an observed result written in visible text.

It never opens a source file. It doesn't take the target path at all. The skill says this itself, in one line of Phase 4: validator success "proves format and ledger consistency only." A hunter's observed result is a string, and my invented one was schema-valid.

A cheap check gets one

Next I wrote 15 lines of Node that open every cited file and check the line exists:

ok   admin/export-xff-gate
ok   notes/note-sql-concat
ok   notes/search-sql-concat
FAIL users/find-user-template-sql  src/routes/login.js: no such file; src/users.js: no such file

That kills the invented file. Cloudflare's harness has the same idea in plain code: per the blog, deterministic code confirms the cited files and paths exist before a finding moves on.

It does nothing for the getNote claim. Line 24 is real, and it really runs a query with the id in it. Every fact the record cites is true except the one that matters.

The skeptic gets the rest

So I walked the Phase 3 prompt by hand. Step 2 says to rebuild the strongest control on the path. For getNote that takes one read: id and owner are bound as placeholders. Step 3 says to reproduce the minimum result yourself. My service is my own code with dummy data, so I ran it on loopback (the skill demands an OS-enforced sandbox before it runs anyone else's target; this was not that). Output trimmed:

search, normal     200 [{"id":1,"title":"groceries"}]
search, payload    200 [{"id":1,"title":"groceries"},{"id":2,"title":"payroll"}]
note, bob id       200 null
note, payload      200 null
note, payload 2    200 null
export, XFF 10.    200 [... both users' notes ...]

The search payload ' OR 1=1 -- hands alice the title of bob's note. Every getNote payload returns nothing. The export gate opens to a header alone, but whether a client can send that header in production depends on a proxy the repo doesn't contain, so it stays needs_validation with an owner check attached. That is the skill's rule for a deployment fact, and I agree with it.

The final file: one confirmed, one needs validation, two rejected.

$ node validate-findings.cjs findings.json
PASS: 4 findings valid

Same validator, same four fingerprints, same PASS. In between, two of the three "confirmed" bugs became rejected. Only reading the code at the cited line and running the payload told the files apart.

Why the skeptic is the expensive part

Finding candidates is cheap now. Cloudflare's blog reports 20,799 raw candidates from their discovery harness, of which about 12,057 survived validation, and an early validation rejection rate of 40% before better recon brought it down to 11%. At 40%, a team without a refuter gets four bad tickets in every ten. Somebody pays for those, and it's usually a maintainer.

That is also the theme of OpenAI's "Patch the Planet" post on coordinating disclosure as agents surface critical bugs, which was on the Hacker News front page the same day.

So my claim: when you judge an AI security tool, judge the step that tries to prove the finding wrong. The hunt is a hypothesis generator. The product is the record that survived.

Where it falls short

Cost is real. In the Hacker News thread, jesse_dot_id reported at least 150k tokens on a fairly small FastAPI project before hitting a session limit. Issue #20 is a blind test on one seeded target, three rounds per arm, by a team with its own competing tool, which it discloses. There the quick profile cost a median $29.95 against $2.06 for one plain agent, and found the same share of the seeded bugs (a median recall of 0.467 for both). On a small, clean target the skeptic may have nothing to kill.

And a skeptic that shares the hunter's model is not fully independent. Per that same issue, the skill's verifiers inherit the session's model. Cloudflare's own pipeline triages with a different model from the one that hunts. Fresh context is not a different mind.

If you run AI reviews on your code today, what does the step that tries to disprove a finding look like: a second model, a test that must fail before the fix, or you?

articles.title: I Got Tired of Switching Tools While Coding on My Phone, So I Built This
articles.description: Hey everyone!  I made a web framework called Authtics Host, also known as HostJS, and one of the...
articles.body_html:
Hey everyone!

I made a web framework called Authtics Host, also known as HostJS, and one of the things I'm most proud of is its built-in Developer Panel.

The reason I wanted this is pretty simple: I develop stuff on my phone. 💀

When you're developing a website, you need to check logs, investigate requests, see what's happening on the server, and figure out why something isn't working. Switching between tools just to do that gets annoying pretty quickly on a phone.

So I wanted those tools available right inside the framework I'm already using.

That's where the Developer Panel comes in.

What is Authtics Host?

Authtics Host is a web framework inspired by Next.js. It uses TypeScript, TSX, React, and Esbuild, and supports SSR (Server-Side Rendering), SSG (Static Site Generation), CSR (Client-Side Rendering), and SRTWS (Site Rendering Through WebSockets, which is currently in beta).

I'm still working on improving it, but I wanted to share one of its features that has genuinely helped me while developing.

Getting started

First, you'll need Node.js 22.

Install Authtics Host using npm:

npm install @bananacool467/authtics-host@latest

For a basic project, you can use a structure like this:

my-project/
├── index.ts
├── authtics_host.config.ts
└── client/
    └── pages/
        └── index.tsx

In index.ts, create the app:

import { App } from "@bananacool467/authtics-host";

const app = new App();

Then configure the framework in authtics_host.config.ts:

import { defineConfig } from "@bananacool467/authtics-host";

export default defineConfig({
  port: 8000,
  renderType: "ssr",
  devMode: true,
  autoFile: true,
  autoPage: true,
  autoPageDir: "client/pages",
  autoFileDir: "client/public"
});

Finally, create client/pages/index.tsx:

export default function Index() {
  return (
    <p>Hello, World!</p>
  );
}

Start the project with:

node --experimental-strip-types index.ts

You should get your page, and with development mode enabled, you should also see a clickable Developer Panel at the bottom-right.

So, what's in the Developer Panel?

The panel has eight tabs:

  • Console — View current logs.
  • Route — Check information about the current route.
  • Webpage Info — See information about the current webpage.
  • Network — Check the current ping and inspect fetch requests sent from the client and responses received from the server.
  • Client Info — View the client's user agent, operating system, and FPS.
  • About Host — Check the current Authtics Host version.
  • Server Info — Check server heap usage, CPU usage, request count, connected users, and uptime.
  • Panel Customization — Customize the Developer Panel.

Here's what it looks like:


The panel gives you somewhere to look when you're trying to figure out what's going on with your application, without having to keep switching to a separate tool for every little thing.

For example, if a request isn't behaving the way you expected, you can check the Network tab. If you're trying to figure out what the application is logging, you can check the Console tab.

You also have route and client information available when you need it.

Obviously, this doesn't mean you will never need other debugging tools. It's just convenient to have these features available in the framework itself.

It can do more than inspect things

The Developer Panel also has controls for managing the running app.

Depending on how you've configured access, you can restart or shut down the app and pause or resume incoming users.

That can be useful when you're testing something and need to control what's happening without going off to manage the server separately.

A quick note about developer access

The panel uses something called a DAT (Developer Access Token).

If you configure a DAT in authtics_host.config.ts, you can restrict developer access using a token you specify:

export default defineConfig({
  port: 8000,
  renderType: "ssr",
  devMode: true,
  dat: "YOUR DAT HERE"
});

Replace YOUR DAT HERE with your own token. Don't publish a real token in your source code or share it publicly.

You can also configure an array of DATs if multiple developers need access.

Without a DAT restriction configured, the panel only provides access to the Console and Network tabs. Setting a DAT restriction enables access to the other developer features, including the app management controls.

Since the panel can expose information about your app and provide controls over the server, make sure you configure access appropriately before deploying anything publicly. You can also turn the panel off by setting devMode to false.

Why I built it this way

This is the part that matters most to me.

I didn't build the Developer Panel just to have another feature to list in a README. I built it because I actually use it.

When you're coding on a phone, little inconveniences add up. Having the console, network information, client details, and server information in one place means I don't have to keep interrupting my workflow to go somewhere else just to investigate what's happening.

And that's really the goal of Authtics Host: make web development more convenient, especially for people working from mobile devices.

I'm not saying this will magically make every developer faster, or that everyone needs another framework. I built something that solves a problem I personally ran into, and the Developer Panel has helped me with my own work.

That's a pretty good reason for me to keep improving it.

Try it out

Authtics Host is available on npm:

https://www.npmjs.com/package/@bananacool467/authtics-host

The package includes more than just the Developer Panel, so check out the README for the other framework features and configuration options.

If you try it, I'd genuinely like to hear what works for you and what needs improvement. Feedback is useful, especially while the project is still evolving.

Thanks for reading!

articles.title: Can AI Crawlers See Your JavaScript? A 10-Minute curl Test for the HTML Bots Actually Get
articles.description: Your page looks perfect in Chrome. Headline, pricing, FAQ, a nice comparison table. But an AI crawler...
articles.body_html:
Your page looks perfect in Chrome. Headline, pricing, FAQ, a nice comparison table. But an AI crawler doesn't open Chrome. It sends one HTTP request, gets back whatever your server returns, and moves on.

If your important text only appears after JavaScript runs, there's a real chance that crawler saw an empty shell. This post shows how to check that in about ten minutes with curl and a couple of one-liners.

Why this matters for AI search

There are two versions of every page:

  1. The initial HTML - what the server sends in response to a request.
  2. The rendered page - what you see after scripts run, APIs return data and widgets load.

Google documents a separate rendering stage for JavaScript (JavaScript SEO basics). Other clients don't have to copy Google's capabilities. In December 2024, Vercel and MERJ published an analysis of AI crawler traffic on Vercel's network (The rise of the AI crawler). They found that OpenAI's crawlers, ClaudeBot, PerplexityBot and several others fetched JavaScript files but didn't execute them, while Gemini (via Google's infrastructure) and Applebot did render pages. Crawler behavior can change over time, so treat this as a reason to test, not as a permanent rule.

The safe assumption: if a fact isn't in the initial HTML, don't count on an AI crawler seeing it.

Step 1: Pick three pages, not your whole site

Don't start with a full crawl. Choose:

  • a service or pricing page,
  • one article or guide,
  • one product or listing page.

For each one, write down 3-5 facts that must be visible: the H1, the main description, a price or condition, a key claim, and the important internal links.

Step 2: Fetch the raw HTML 

URL="https://example.com/pricing"

curl -sL "$URL" -o raw.html
wc -c raw.html

Ignore the file size. A 300 KB response can be all navigation and inline JSON; a 20 KB response can contain the full answer. What matters is meaning.

To see the response a specific crawler would get, you can also send its user agent string (useful when a CDN or WAF treats bots differently):

curl -sL -A "Mozilla/5.0 AppleWebKit/537.36 (KHTML, like Gecko; compatible; GPTBot/1.1; +https://openai.com/gptbot)" \
  -o raw_gptbot.html -w "%{http_code}\n" "$URL"

If this returns 403, 429 or a challenge page while a normal request returns 200, you have a different problem: your firewall, not your rendering. Fix that first.

Step 3: Search for your must-have facts 

for phrase in "Pricing" "per month" "Free trial" "How it works"; do
  if grep -qi "$phrase" raw.html; then
    echo "FOUND:   $phrase"
  else
    echo "MISSING: $phrase"
  fi
done

A match isn't the whole story. Text sitting inside a JSON blob in a <script> tag (for example __NEXT_DATA__ or a hydration payload) is technically "in the HTML," but a normal content extractor may not treat it as the main content. (The Vercel study notes that models can sometimes interpret JSON in the initial response, but you shouldn't rely on it.) Check where the match lives:

grep -o -i ".\{80\}per month.\{80\}" raw.html | head

If every hit is inside a script, mark it as "present in data, not in markup."

Step 4: Strip the markup and read it like a bot

A quick way to see the visible text without a browser:

python3 - <<'PY'
import re, html
t = open("raw.html", encoding="utf-8", errors="ignore").read()
t = re.sub(r"(?is)<(script|style|noscript|svg)[^>]*>.*?</\1>", " ", t)
t = re.sub(r"(?s)<[^>]+>", " ", t)
t = re.sub(r"\s+", " ", html.unescape(t)).strip()
print(len(t.split()), "words")
print(t[:1500])
PY

Read the first 1,500 characters. Does it say what the page is about and what you offer? Or is it "Loading... Menu Sign in Cookie settings"?

Step 5: Compare with the rendered page

Open the same URL in your browser, open DevTools and compare the rendered DOM with raw.html. Note which important elements only exist after load: tabs, accordions filled by API calls, pricing tables from a widget, reviews from a third-party script.

Also test direct URL access. Single-page apps sometimes work when you click from the homepage but return a generic shell (or a 404) when the route is requested directly. Crawlers always request directly.

Step 6: Fix delivery, not the content

If the useful text is missing from the initial HTML, the usual options are:

  • Server-side rendering (SSR) for pages that change often.
  • Static generation / prerendering for pages that change rarely.
  • Moving critical facts into the server-rendered template (H1, intro, price, key FAQ answers) while keeping interactive extras client-side.

Don't build a separate "bot version" with different claims. Visitors and crawlers should get the same meaning; serving different content to bots is the kind of thing that backfires.

Step 7: Save before and after

When the fix ships, re-run the same curl and the same checks. Keep both files:

curl -sL "$URL" -o "after_$(date +%F).html"

A fix is done when the main text is present in a direct request, the page still works for humans, and the required links are there. That removes a technical barrier. It doesn't make the page relevant to every question or guarantee a citation, so track discovery and citations separately.

A quick checklist

  • [ ] Three representative pages chosen
  • [ ] Must-have facts listed per page
  • [ ] Raw HTML fetched (normal UA and crawler UA)
  • [ ] Status codes match between the two
  • [ ] Facts found in markup, not only in script data
  • [ ] Direct URL access tested for app routes
  • [ ] Fix verified with a before/after snapshot

If you want this check done automatically, AURA GEO audits the HTML your server actually returns, flags pages where little readable text comes through, and turns that into tasks you can hand to your own agent over MCP.
